author: Decemviri
source_text: Si in ius vocat, ito. Ni it, antestamino. Igitur em capito.
question: Quid facere debet, ex lege duodecim tabularum, is quem quis in ius vocat?
question_en: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, what must a man do whom someone summons to court?
derivation: The opening command of the whole code: si in ius vocat, ito. The Tables were memorized by schoolboys (Cicero, De legibus 2.59), and this incipit is the most-quoted line of archaic Roman law. Anchored to the named law; single supported answer (ito).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si in ius vocat, ito. Ni it, antestamino. Igitur em capito.
question: Quid facere debet qui in ius vocat, antequam vocatum ire nolentem capiat, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, what must the summoner do before he seizes a man who, summoned to court, refuses to go?
derivation: Procedure of tab. I: ni it, antestamino; igitur em capito — first call witnesses, only then lay hold of him. The antestatio was ambient legal culture (cf. Horace, Sermones 1.9.76 'licet antestari?'). Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si calvitur pedemve struit, manum endo iacito.
question: Quid ei licet qui in ius vocat, si vocatus calvitur pedemve struit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What may the summoner do under the Law of the Twelve Tables if the man summoned shirks or takes to flight?
derivation: Tab. I on the evasive defendant: si calvitur pedemve struit, manum endo iacito — the archaic clause glossed by Festus. The permitted act (laying on of the hand) is the single supported answer; anchored to the named law and the defined situation.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si morbus aevitasve vitium escit, iumentum dato.
question: Quid dari lex duodecim tabularum iubet, si morbus aevitasve eum qui in ius vocatur impedit?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables order to be provided if sickness or age hinders the man summoned to court?
derivation: The humane transport clause of tab. I, discussed at length by Gellius 20.1.25-29: if illness or age is the impediment, the summoner must supply a iumentum. Single named-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si morbus aevitasve vitium escit, iumentum dato. Si nolet, arceram ne sternito.
question: Quale vehiculum aegro vocato sternere non cogitur is qui in ius vocat, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What kind of vehicle is the summoner not obliged to furnish for a sick man he has summoned, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Counterpart of the iumentum clause: si nolet, arceram ne sternito — he need not spread the cushioned covered cart. The arcera is glossed from this very clause by Gellius 20.1.29-30. Single named-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Assiduo vindex assiduus esto. Proletario iam civi quis volet vindex esto.
question: Qualis vindex assiduo esse debet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What sort of surety (vindex) must a landholder have under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: A landholder (an assiduus, one of his own class).
derivation: The class rule on the vindex, quoted by Gellius 16.10.5: for an assiduus the surety must be an assiduus. Anchored to the named law and the named class; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Assiduo vindex assiduus esto. Proletario iam civi quis volet vindex esto.
question: Quis proletario civi vindex esse potest ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Who may act as surety (vindex) for a proletarian citizen under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Second half of the vindex rule: for the proletarius, quis volet — any volunteer suffices. The assiduus/proletarius contrast made this clause a standard citation (Gellius 16.10). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Ni pacunt, in comitio aut in foro ante meridiem caussam coiciunto.
question: Quibus locis litigantes, ni pacunt, causam coicere debent ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: In which places must the litigants, if they do not settle, state their case under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: In the comitium or in the forum.
derivation: Venue rule of tab. I: failing a settlement, the case is pleaded in comitio aut in foro. Two named civic places form the complete supported answer; anchored to the named law.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Ni pacunt, in comitio aut in foro ante meridiem caussam coiciunto.
question: Quo tempore diei litigantes causam coicere iubentur ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: At what time of day are the litigants ordered to state their case under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Time rule of the same clause: the pleading happens ante meridiem. Single time answer supported verbatim; pairs with the post-meridiem default judgment that follows.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Com peroranto ambo praesentes. Post meridiem praesenti litem addicito.
question: Cui litem post meridiem addici lex duodecim tabularum iubet, si alter litigantium abest?
question_en: To whom does the Law of the Twelve Tables order the suit to be awarded after midday, if one of the litigants is absent?
derivation: The default-judgment rule: post meridiem praesenti litem addicito — after noon, judgment goes to whichever party showed up. Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si ambo praesentes, solis occasus suprema tempestas esto.
question: Quae est, ex lege duodecim tabularum, suprema tempestas qua iudicium finiri debet?
question_en: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, what is the latest hour (suprema tempestas) by which court proceedings must end?
derivation: The celebrated court deadline: solis occasus suprema tempestas esto — sunset closes the day's proceedings. Quoted by Gellius 17.2.10 and proverbial in legal culture. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Actor dicito: ex sponsione te mihi . . . dare oportere aio. Quando tu negas, te praetor iudicem sive arbitrum postulo uti des.
question: A quo actor, ex lege duodecim tabularum, iudicem sive arbitrum dari postulat, quando reus negat?
question_en: From whom, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, does the plaintiff demand that a judge or arbiter be given, when the defendant denies the claim?
derivation: The formula of the legis actio per iudicis arbitrive postulationem (cf. Gaius, Inst. 4.17a): the plaintiff addresses the praetor — te praetor iudicem sive arbitrum postulo uti des. The named magistracy is the single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: . . . morbus sonticus . . . aut status dies cum hoste . . . quid horum fuit unum iudici arbitrove reove, eo dies diffissus esto.
question: Quid fit de die iudicii, si morbus sonticus aut status dies cum hoste iudici arbitrove reove fuit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What happens to the trial day under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a grave illness, or a day appointed with a foreigner, has befallen the judge, the arbiter, or the defendant?
answer_en: The day is broken off (the hearing is postponed).
derivation: Adjournment clause of tab. II: morbus sonticus or a status dies cum hoste splits the trial day (dies diffissus esto). Cicero, De officiis 1.37 quotes status dies cum hoste to show hostis anciently meant the foreigner. Single supported outcome.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Cui testimonium defuerit, is tertiis diebus ob portum obvagulatum ito.
question: Quibus diebus is, cui testimonium defuerit, ob portum testis obvagulatum ire iubetur ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: On which days is the man whose witness has failed him ordered to go wail before that witness's doorway, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The obvagulatio: the party let down by his witness goes every third day to howl before the defaulter's door (portus = house door, Festus). The interval tertiis diebus is the single supported answer; the picturesque rite made the clause memorable.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Aeris confessi rebusque iure iudicatis XXX dies iusti sunto.
question: Quot dies iusti debitori aeris confessi rebusque iure iudicatis lege duodecim tabularum dantur?
question_en: How many days of grace does the Law of the Twelve Tables give a debtor after admission of the debt or lawful judgment?
derivation: The famous thirty iusti dies of grace before execution on a confessed or adjudged debt (Gellius 20.1.42-43 explains them). Anchored to the named law; single number answer supported verbatim (XXX).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Post deinde manus iniectio esto. In ius ducito.
question: Quid debitori imminet ex lege duodecim tabularum, cum triginta dies iusti praeterierunt nec iudicatum fecit?
question_en: What awaits the debtor under the Law of the Twelve Tables once the thirty days of grace have passed and he has not satisfied the judgment?
answer_en: The laying-on of hands (manus iniectio — personal seizure).
derivation: Sequence of tab. III: after the thirty days, post deinde manus iniectio esto — the creditor seizes the debtor and hales him in ius. The named institution is the single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Ni iudicatum facit aut quis endo eo in iure vindicit, secum ducito, vincito aut nervo aut compedibus XV pondo, ne maiore aut si volet minore vincito.
question: Quot pondo plurimum compedibus debitor addictus vinciri potest ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: With fetters of how many pounds at most may a bound-over debtor be shackled under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: Fifteen pounds (no heavier; lighter if the creditor wishes).
derivation: The fetter-weight cap of tab. III: compedibus XV pondo, ne maiore. Gellius 20.1.45 quotes the clause. Single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si volet suo vivito, ni suo vivit, qui eum vinctum habebit, libras faris endo dies dato.
question: Quantum farris in dies debitori vincto, qui suo non vivit, dare debet qui eum vinctum habet?
question_en: How much spelt per day must the creditor who holds a debtor in bonds give him, if the debtor does not live at his own expense?
answer_en: A pound of spelt (far) a day.
derivation: The maintenance clause of tab. III: the creditor must give libras faris endo dies — a pound of far daily — to the imprisoned debtor who has no means of his own (Gellius 20.1.45). Single measure answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Erat autem ius interea paciscendi ac nisi pacti forent habebantur in vinculis dies LX.
question: Quot dies debitores addicti, nisi pacti erant, in vinculis habebantur, ut Gellius de lege duodecim tabularum tradit?
question_en: For how many days were bound-over debtors kept in chains if no settlement was reached, as Gellius reports of the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Gellius 20.1.46 (quoted in the text) on the debt procedure: sixty days in chains with the right to settle meanwhile. Attributed to Gellius since the number comes from his account of the law; single number answer supported verbatim (dies LX).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Inter eos dies trinis nundinis continuis ad praetorem in comitium producebantur, quantaeque pecuniae iudicati essent, praedicabatur.
question: Quo debitores vincti trinis nundinis continuis producebantur, ut Gellius de lege duodecim tabularum tradit?
question_en: Where were the imprisoned debtors brought out on three successive market-days, as Gellius reports of the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: Before the praetor, into the comitium.
derivation: Gellius 20.1.46: during the sixty days the debtor was produced ad praetorem in comitium on three successive nundinae and the judgment debt proclaimed. Named magistrate and place form the supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Tertiis autem nundinis capite poenas dabant,aut trans Tiberim peregre venum ibant.
question: Quo debitores addicti, qui tertiis nundinis non soluti erant, venum ibant, ut Gellius de lege duodecim tabularum tradit?
question_en: Where were bound-over debtors who had not been released by the third market-day sold, as Gellius reports of the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: Across the Tiber, abroad (into foreign slavery).
derivation: Gellius 20.1.47: on the third nundinae the debtor paid with his life or went trans Tiberim peregre venum — sold beyond the Tiber, i.e. out of Roman territory. The phrase trans Tiberim became proverbial for that fate; single place answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Tertiis nundinis partis secanto.
question: Quibus nundinis creditoribus partes debitoris secare licet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: On which market-day may the creditors cut their portions of the debtor, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The most notorious clause of the Tables: tertiis nundinis partis secanto — on the third nundinae the creditors may cut their shares. Gellius 20.1.48-52 discusses it with horror and notes no case was recorded. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si plus minusve secuerunt, se fraude esto
question: Quid iuris est ex lege duodecim tabularum, si creditores partes debitoris secantes plus minusve secuerunt?
question_en: What is the legal position under the Law of the Twelve Tables if creditors, cutting their portions of the debtor, have cut more or less than their share?
answer_en: It is without liability (se fraude esto — no penalty attaches).
derivation: The chilling coda to partis secanto: si plus minusve secuerunt, se fraude esto — cutting too much or too little carries no liability. Quoted verbatim by Gellius 20.1.49 and by Quintilian 3.6.84; the answer normalizes archaic se fraude to sine fraude.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. III (al. tab. VI 4)
source_text: adversus hostem aeterna auctoritas esto.
question: Qualis est, ex lege duodecim tabularum, auctoritas adversus hostem, id est peregrinum?
question_en: Of what duration, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, is the warranty of ownership (auctoritas) against a hostis, that is, a foreigner?
answer_en: Eternal (it never lapses — a foreigner can never usucapt).
derivation: The maxim adversus hostem aeterna auctoritas, quoted by Cicero, De officiis 1.37, who explains that hostis in the Tables means the foreigner: against a stranger the owner's claim never expires by usucapion. Printed under tab. III in this edition (traditionally tab. VI 4). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si pater filium ter venum duit, filius a patre liber esto.
question: Quotiens pater filium venum dare debet, ut filius a patre liber sit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: How many times must a father sell his son for the son to be free of the father, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The celebrated thrice-sold-son rule, the foundation of Roman emancipatio and adoption procedure (Gaius, Inst. 1.132 builds on it). Anchored to the named law; single number answer supported verbatim (ter).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Uti legassit super pecunia tutelave suae rei, ita ius esto.
question: Quae lex sanxit, uti quisque super pecunia tutelave suae rei legasset, ita ius esset?
question_en: Which law ordained that as a man had disposed by will concerning his property or the guardianship of his estate, so should it be law?
answer_en: The Law of the Twelve Tables.
derivation: The charter of Roman freedom of testation — uti legassit suae rei, ita ius esto — cited in these words by Cicero (De inventione 2.148) and the jurists ever after. The maxim itself is the famous fact, so the question asks which law carries it; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si intestato moritur, cui suus heres nec escit, adgnatus proximus familiam habeto.
question: Quis familiam habet ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis intestato moritur cui suus heres non est?
question_en: Who takes the estate under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man dies intestate leaving no direct heir (suus heres)?
derivation: The intestate-succession rule: failing a suus heres, adgnatus proximus familiam habeto. The backbone of Roman inheritance law, endlessly cited by the jurists (Gaius, Inst. 3.9). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si adgnatus nec escit, gentiles familiam habento.
question: Quis familiam habet ex lege duodecim tabularum, si intestato mortuo nec suus heres nec adgnatus est?
question_en: Who takes the estate under the Law of the Twelve Tables if an intestate leaves neither a direct heir nor an agnate?
answer_en: The members of his gens (the gentiles).
derivation: Third rung of the intestate ladder: si adgnatus nec escit, gentiles familiam habento. The succession of the gentiles is a standard cited feature of archaic law (Gaius, Inst. 3.17). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. V 6 (Gaius, Inst. 1.155)
source_text: Quibus testamento...tutor datus non sit, iis lege XII Tabularum agnati sunt tutores.
question: Qui sunt ex lege duodecim tabularum tutores iis, quibus testamento tutor datus non est, ut Gaius tradit?
question_en: Who, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, are the guardians of those to whom no guardian has been given by will, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius, Inst. 1.155 (quoted in the text): failing a testamentary tutor, the agnates are tutores legitimi by the Twelve Tables — the tutela rule governing women and children. Attributed to Gaius; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si furiosus escit, adgnatum gentiliumque in eo pecuniaque eius potestas esto.
question: Penes quos est, ex lege duodecim tabularum, potestas in furiosum pecuniamque eius?
question_en: In whose hands, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, is the power over a madman and his property?
answer_en: In the hands of his agnates and the members of his gens.
derivation: The famous provision on the furiosus: power over him and his money belongs to the agnates and gentiles — the origin of the cura furiosi, cited by Cicero (De inventione 2.148) and the Rhetorica ad Herennium 1.23. Two-item supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Cum nexum faciet mancipiumque, uti lingua nuncupassit, ita ius esto.
question: Quid in nexo mancipioque faciendo vim iuris habet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: In making a nexum or a mancipium, what has the force of law under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: What the tongue has solemnly declared (the spoken declaration).
derivation: The maxim uti lingua nuncupassit, ita ius esto: the oral declaration in nexum and mancipium binds as law. Quoted by Festus (nuncupata pecunia) and echoed by Cicero, De officiis 3.65. Short supported answer stating the source of legal force.

author: Decemviri
source_text: tignum iunctum aedibus vineave sei concapit ne solvito
question: Quid de tigno aedibus vineave iuncto lex duodecim tabularum iubet?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables command concerning a beam built into a house or a vineyard?
answer_en: That it not be detached (the built-in beam may not be removed).
derivation: The tignum iunctum rule: a beam (or vine-prop) once built into another's structure may not be pried out — the basis of the actio de tigno iuncto (Ulpian, D. 47.3.1, citing the Tables). The command ne solvito is the single supported answer; the mutilated continuation (duplione) is not relied on.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. VI (Gaius, Inst. 1.111)
source_text: Lege XII tabularum cautum est, ut si qua nollet usu in manum mariti convenire, ea quotannis trinoctio abesset atque eo modo cuiusque anni usum interrumperet.
question: Quamdiu quotannis abesse debebat uxor, quae usu in manum mariti convenire nollet, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: For how long each year did a wife have to stay away, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, if she did not wish to pass into her husband's manus by usus?
derivation: Gaius, Inst. 1.111 (quoted in the text): a year's uninterrupted usus brought the wife into manus, and the Tables let her interrupt it by an annual absence of three nights — the famous trinoctium. Single duration answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: ambitus . . . sestertius pes
question: Quantus est ambitus, id est spatium circum aedificia relinquendum, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
answer: Sestertius pes, id est duo pedes et semis.
question_en: How wide is the ambitus, the strip to be left clear around buildings, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: A sestertius pes, that is, two and a half feet.
derivation: The boundary-strip rule of tab. VII: the ambitus around buildings measured sestertius pes — 'a half-third foot', i.e. 2 1/2 feet (so Varro, De lingua Latina 5.22 and Festus gloss both words from this clause). The fragment juxtaposes term and measure; single measure answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si iurgant . . . tres arbitri . . .
question: Quot arbitri dantur ex lege duodecim tabularum, si vicini de finibus iurgant?
question_en: How many arbiters are appointed under the Law of the Twelve Tables when neighbors quarrel over their boundaries?
derivation: The boundary-dispute clause: si iurgant — Cicero, De legibus 1.55 attests that iurgium in the Tables is precisely the neighbors' quarrel over fines — three arbiters are given to settle it. Single number answer supported by the fragment.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Viam muniunto: ni sam delapidassint, qua volet iumento agito.
question: Qua iumento agere licet ei qui via utitur, si qui viam munire debent eam lapidibus non straverunt, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Where may a man drive his beast, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, if those obliged to maintain a road have not paved it with stones?
derivation: The road-maintenance rule: viam muniunto — and if the owners have not laid it with stone (ni sam delapidassint), the traveler may drive his team qua volet, over the adjoining land. A celebrated servitude rule (cf. Festus on viae); the supported answer is the law's own phrase.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Qui malum carmen incantassit . . .
question: Quae lex Romana de eo cavit, qui malum carmen incantasset?
question_en: Which Roman law made provision against one who had chanted an evil spell (malum carmen)?
answer_en: The Law of the Twelve Tables.
derivation: The malum carmen clause opens tab. VIII; only the protasis survives here, so the pair asks which law carried the famous provision. Its celebrity is attested by Pliny, NH 28.18 and Cicero (apud Augustinum, De civitate Dei 2.9), who debate whether it aimed at spells or lampoons. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto.
question: Quae poena est ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis membrum alteri rupit nec cum eo pacit?
question_en: What is the penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man has maimed another's limb and does not come to terms with him?
derivation: The talion clause — si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto — the most famous penal provision of the Tables, quoted by Festus and discussed by Gellius 20.1.14-38. Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto.
question: Quo uno modo talionem effugit, qui membrum alteri rupit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: By what single means does a man who has maimed another's limb escape retaliation, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: By settlement — if he comes to terms with the victim.
derivation: The escape clause inside the talion provision: ni cum eo pacit — talio applies only failing a compact with the injured party. The primacy of composition over vengeance is the standard point drawn from this clause (Gellius 20.1.38). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Manu fustive si os fregit libero, CCC assium, si servo, CL assium poenam subito
question: Quot assium poenam subit ex lege duodecim tabularum, qui manu fustive os libero fregit?
question_en: What fine in asses does a man incur under the Law of the Twelve Tables for breaking a free man's bone with hand or club?
derivation: The os fractum tariff: 300 asses for a free man's broken bone. Quoted by Gellius 20.1.12 and Gaius (D. 47.10.7); the free/slave differential made it a textbook citation. Single number answer supported verbatim (CCC).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Manu fustive si os fregit libero, CCC assium, si servo, CL assium poenam subito
question: Quot assium poenam subit ex lege duodecim tabularum, qui manu fustive os servo fregit?
question_en: What fine in asses does a man incur under the Law of the Twelve Tables for breaking a slave's bone with hand or club?
derivation: Second half of the os fractum tariff: 150 asses when the victim is a slave — exactly half the free man's rate, the celebrated status differential of archaic delict law. Single number answer supported verbatim (CL).

author: Decemviri
source_text: si iniuriam faxsit, viginti quinque poenae asses sunto.
question: Quot asses poenae sunt ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis iniuriam alteri fecit?
question_en: How many asses is the penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man has committed a simple outrage (iniuria) against another?
derivation: The 25-as fine for iniuria, made famous by Gellius 20.1.13: L. Veratius strolled about slapping free men while a slave paid out the twenty-five asses on the spot — the anecdote that showed the tariff obsolete. Single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: rupsit . . . sarcito.
question: Quid eum, qui rupit, id est damnum dedit, lex duodecim tabularum facere iubet?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables order the man who has 'broken' — that is, done damage — to do?
answer_en: To make it good (repair the loss).
derivation: The damnum kernel rupsit... sarcito: whoever damages must make whole. Festus glosses rupitias = damnum dederit and sarcito = solvito, praestato from this clause, the ancestor of the law of damage later covered by the lex Aquilia. The two surviving words state protasis and remedy; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Qui fruges excantassit . . . neve alienam segetem pellexeris . . . capite.
question: Qua poena lex duodecim tabularum eum adficit, qui fruges excantavit alienamve segetem pellexit?
question_en: With what penalty does the Law of the Twelve Tables strike the man who has charmed away the crops or lured off another's harvest by spells?
derivation: The crop-magic clauses (fruges excantare, segetem pellicere), punished capitally — Pliny, NH 28.17-18 cites both, and the acquittal of C. Furius Cresimus on this very charge (NH 18.41-43) kept them famous. 'Capite' is the edition's supplement printed with the fragment (brackets stripped per guidelines). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: si nox furtum faxsit, si occisit, iure caesus esto.
question: Quid iuris est ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis furem nocturnum occidit?
question_en: What is the legal position under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man has killed a thief in the night?
answer_en: The thief is lawfully slain (the killing is lawful).
derivation: The night-thief clause: si nox furtum faxsit, si occisit, iure caesus esto — the nocturnal thief may be killed with impunity. Quoted by Macrobius, Sat. 1.4.19 and Cicero, Pro Milone 9; the day/night contrast is the celebrated point. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Luci . . . si se telo defendit, . . . endoque plorato.
question: Quo solo casu furem luci deprehensum occidere licet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: In what single case may a thief caught by daylight be killed under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: Only if he defends himself with a weapon.
derivation: Counterpart of the night-thief rule: by day (luci) the thief may be killed only si se telo defendit, and the killer must raise the cry (endoque plorato). Attested by Gaius (D. 9.2.4.1) and Cicero, Pro Milone 9. The condition is the single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Lance et licio ito.
question: Quibus rebus instructus furtum in aliena domo quaerere debet, qui ex lege duodecim tabularum quaerit?
question_en: Equipped with what objects must a man search another's house for stolen goods, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: With a dish and a loincloth (lanx et licium).
derivation: The ritual search quaestio lance licioque: the searcher enters girt only with a licium, holding a lanx. Described — and mocked as absurd — by Gaius, Inst. 3.192-193, and discussed by Gellius 11.18.9 and Festus; one of the most famous curiosities of the Tables. Two-item supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si adorat furto, quod nec manifestum erit . . ., duplione damnum decidito.
question: Quanti damnum decidere debet fur ex lege duodecim tabularum, cuius furtum nec manifestum est?
question_en: At what rate must a thief settle the loss under the Law of the Twelve Tables when his theft is not manifest?
derivation: The furtum nec manifestum tariff: double damages (duplione damnum decidito), against the fourfold or capital consequences of manifest theft — the classic distinction reported by Gaius, Inst. 3.190-191 from the Tables. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Patronus si clienti fraudem fecerit, sacer esto.
question: Quid fit patronus ex lege duodecim tabularum, si clienti fraudem fecerit?
question_en: What does a patron become under the Law of the Twelve Tables if he has wronged his client?
answer_en: Accursed (sacer — forfeited to the gods, an outlaw).
derivation: The patronage clause: patronus si clienti fraudem fecerit, sacer esto — the faithless patron becomes sacer, killable without penalty. Quoted by Servius (ad Aen. 6.609); the sanctity of the patron-client bond is core Roman social knowledge. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Qui se sierit testarier libripensve fuerit, ni testimonium fatiatur, inprobus intestabilisque esto.
question: Quid fit ex lege duodecim tabularum, qui testis libripensve fuit neque testimonium fatetur?
question_en: What becomes of a man, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, who has acted as witness or scale-holder and then refuses to bear his testimony?
answer_en: Dishonored and disqualified from witnessing (improbus intestabilisque).
derivation: The perfidious-witness clause, quoted by Gellius 15.13.11: whoever served as testis or libripens in a formal act and will not vouch for it becomes inprobus intestabilisque — the origin of the proverbial word intestabilis. Two-word supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si telum manu fugit magis quam iecit, arietem subicito.
question: Quid subicere debet ex lege duodecim tabularum is, cuius telum manu fugit magis quam iecit?
question_en: What must a man offer in substitution, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, if his weapon flew from his hand rather than being thrown?
derivation: The accidental-homicide clause: where the weapon escaped the hand (no intent), a ram is offered in the victim's place — expiation instead of punishment. Cicero cites the clause (Topica 64; Pro Tullio 51), and the ram-substitution is a famous relic of sacral law. Single named-animal answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: privilegia ne inroganto.
question: Quid de privilegiis lex duodecim tabularum sanxit?
question_en: What did the Law of the Twelve Tables ordain concerning privilegia (laws aimed at single individuals)?
answer_en: That they not be enacted (laws against individuals were forbidden).
derivation: The ban on privilegia, cited with pride by Cicero, De legibus 3.11 and 3.44: no law may be proposed against a private individual. Anchored to the named law and the named institution; the prohibition itself is the short supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: de capite civis nisi per maximum comitiatum . . . ne ferunto.
question: Per quem comitiatum solum de capite civis ferri licet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Through which assembly alone may a vote touching the caput (life and status) of a citizen be carried, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: Only through the greatest assembly (the comitiatus maximus, i.e. the comitia centuriata).
derivation: The capital-jurisdiction guarantee: de capite civis only per maximum comitiatum — which Cicero, De legibus 3.11 and 3.44 (cf. De re publica 2.61) identifies with the comitia centuriata. A pillar of the citizen's protections, endlessly invoked in the late Republic. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Hominem mortuum in urbe ne sepelito neve urito.
question: Ubi hominem mortuum sepeliri urive lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: Where does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid a dead man to be buried or burned?
derivation: The most famous funerary provision of Roman law: hominem mortuum in urbe ne sepelito neve urito (quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.58) — the reason Roman tombs line the roads outside the gates. Anchored to the named law; single place answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: hoc plus ne facito: rogum ascea ne polito.
question: Qua re rogum poliri lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: With what tool does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid the funeral pyre to be smoothed?
answer_en: With the adze (ascia) — the pyre wood was to be left rough.
derivation: The funeral-expense limits of tab. X: rogum ascea ne polito — no dressed timber for the pyre, a curb on funerary display quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.59. Single named-tool answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Mulieres genas ne radunto neve lessum funeris ergo habento.
question: Quae duo facere mulieres in funere lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: What two things does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid women to do at a funeral?
answer_en: To tear their cheeks and to raise the ritual wailing (lessus).
derivation: The mourning restraints on women: genas ne radunto (no lacerating the cheeks) neve lessum habento (no wailing-chant), quoted and discussed by Cicero, De legibus 2.59, who puzzles over the archaic word lessus. Complete two-item supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Homine mortuo ne ossa legito, quo post funus faciat.
question: Quid homine mortuo legi vetat lex duodecim tabularum, quo post funus alterum fiat?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid to be gathered from the dead, for the purpose of holding a second funeral later?
derivation: The one-funeral rule: ne ossa legito, quo post funus faciat — the bones may not be collected to stage a later funeral (Cicero, De legibus 2.60 notes the exception for death in war or abroad). Single supported answer (ossa).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Neve aurum addito.
question: Quod metallum cum mortuo poni lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: Which metal does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid to be placed with the dead?
derivation: The grave-goods restriction: neve aurum addito — no gold in the burial, part of the sumptuary program of tab. X quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.60. Single named-metal answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Neve aurum addito. At cui auro dentes iuncti escunt. Ast in cum illo sepeliet uretve, se fraude esto.
question: Quod unum aurum cum mortuo sine fraude sepelire urereve licet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What is the one gold that may lawfully be buried or burned with the dead under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: The gold with which his teeth are bound (dental gold).
derivation: The celebrated exception to the gold ban: teeth fastened with gold may be buried or burned with the body se fraude — without penalty. Cicero, De legibus 2.60 quotes the clause with amusement; earliest evidence for Roman dental prosthetics. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. XI 1 (Cicero, De re publica 2.36-37)
source_text: qui duabus tabulis iniquarum legum additis...conubia haec illi ut ne plebei cum patribus essent, inhumanissima lege sanxerunt.
question: Quorum inter se conubia duae postremae tabulae legum duodecim vetuerunt?
question_en: Marriages between which two orders did the last two of the Twelve Tables forbid?
derivation: The notorious conubium ban of the eleventh table, branded inhumanissima lex by Cicero (De re publica 2.63, quoted in the text) and repealed by the lex Canuleia of 445 BC — a hinge of the Struggle of the Orders and standard Roman historical knowledge. Two-order supported answer.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. XI (Cicero, De re publica 2.36-37)
source_text: Qui Xviri cum X tabulas summa legum aequitate prudentiaque conscripsissent, in annum posterum Xviros alios subrogaverunt
question: Quot tabulas legum priores decemviri summa aequitate conscripserunt, ut Cicero tradit?
question_en: How many tables of laws did the first board of decemvirs draw up with the greatest fairness, as Cicero relates?
derivation: Cicero, De re publica (quoted in the text): the first decemvirate of 451 BC wrote ten tables summa aequitate; the second board added the rest. The 10 + 2 structure of the code is ambient knowledge (cf. Livy 3.34, 3.37). Single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. XI (Cicero, De re publica 2.36-37)
source_text: qui duabus tabulis iniquarum legum additis...conubia haec illi ut ne plebei cum patribus essent, inhumanissima lege sanxerunt.
question: Quot tabulas iniquarum legum posteriores decemviri decem prioribus addiderunt, ut Cicero tradit?
question_en: How many tables of unjust laws did the later decemvirs add to the first ten, as Cicero relates?
derivation: Cicero, De re publica (quoted in the text): the second decemvirate added duabus tabulis iniquarum legum — the two 'unjust tables' completing the twelve. Complements the ten-tables pair; single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si vindiciam falsam tulit, si velit is . . . tor arbitros tris dato
question: Quot arbitri dantur ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis vindiciam falsam tulit?
question_en: How many arbiters are appointed under the Law of the Twelve Tables when a man has carried off a false claim of interim possession (vindicia)?
derivation: The false-vindicia clause: the magistrate (the mutilated '...tor' = praetor) gives three arbiters to assess the wrongful possession. The number tris is clean in the fragment; single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si vindiciam falsam tulit, si velit is . . . tor arbitros tris dato, eorum arbitrio . . . fructus duplione damnum decidito.
question: Quanti damnum decidere debet ex lege duodecim tabularum, qui vindiciam falsam tulit?
question_en: At what rate must the man who carried off a false claim of possession settle the loss, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: At double the fruits (twice the produce of the thing).
derivation: Sanction of the false-vindicia clause: fructus duplione damnum decidito — restitution at double the fruits, by the arbiters' award (cf. Festus s.v. vindiciae). The doubled-fruits measure is the single supported answer.

author: Augustine
source_text: hoc opere instituto et mea ad te promissione debito defendere aduersus eos, qui conditori eius deos suos praeferunt, fili carissime Marcelline, suscepi, magnum opus et arduum, sed Deus adiutor noster est.
question: Cui Augustinus opus De ciuitate Dei in praefatione dedicat atque inscribit?
question_en: To whom does Augustine dedicate and address the work City of God in the preface?
derivation: Preface fact: Augustine undertakes the work as owed by his promise and addresses it to 'fili carissime Marcelline.' Anchored to Augustine + the work; single-name answer (dative Marcellino), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the City of God's dedication to Marcellinus is standard. Source_text normalization: OCR doubling 'defeendere' corrected to 'defendere.'

author: Augustine
source_text: An non etiam illi Romani Christi nomini infesti sunt, quibus propter Christum barbari pepercerunt? Testantur hoc martyrum loca et basilicae apostolorum, quae in illa uastatione Vrbis ad se confugientes suos alienosque receperunt.
question: In quae loca confugientes in illa uastatione Vrbis a barbarorum caede tuti fuerunt, ut Augustinus tradit?
answer: In basilicas apostolorum et martyrum loca.
question_en: Fleeing into which places were people kept safe from the barbarians' slaughter during that sack of the City, as Augustine relates?
answer_en: Into the basilicas of the apostles and the shrines of the martyrs.
derivation: The distinctive claim of Book 1: in the sack of Rome the barbarians spared those who took refuge in the Christian holy places. Anchored to Augustine + the sack of the City (uastatio Vrbis) + the barbari; the answer is the noun phrase supported verbatim ('martyrum loca et basilicae apostolorum'). Closed-book apologetic/historical fact, attributed with 'ut Augustinus tradit.' Note: Book 1 says only 'barbari' (not Goths/Alaric), so the agent is left general as in the text.

author: Augustine
source_text: Lucretiam certe, matronam nobilem ueteremque Romanam, pudicitiae magnis efferunt laudibus. Huius corpore cum uiolenter oppresso Tarquinii regis filius libidinose potitus esset, illa scelus improbissimi iuuenis marito Collatino et propinquo Bruto, uiris clarissimis et fortissimis, indicauit eosque ad uindictam constrinxit.
question: A quo Lucretia, nobilis matrona Romana, uiolenter oppressa atque uitiata est?
question_en: By whom was Lucretia, the noble Roman matron, violently assaulted and ravished?
answer_en: By the son of King Tarquinius.
derivation: The famous Lucretia exemplum. Anchored to Lucretia (named, 'matrona nobilis ueteremque Romana'); single answer identifying the assailant by relation ('Tarquinii regis filius' = the son of King Tarquinius, i.e. Sextus Tarquinius), supported verbatim. Closed-book; the answer is kept to what the text states (the king's son) rather than the proper name Sextus. Source_text normalization: OCR 'uindicatam' corrected to 'uindictam.'

author: Augustine
source_text: illa scelus improbissimi iuuenis marito Collatino et propinquo Bruto, uiris clarissimis et fortissimis, indicauit eosque ad uindictam constrinxit. Deinde foedi in se commissi aegra atque inpatiens se peremit.
question: Quid Lucretia fecit, postquam a Tarquinii regis filio uim perpessa scelus indicauit?
question_en: What did Lucretia do after, having suffered violence from the son of King Tarquinius, she had disclosed the crime?
derivation: The famous suicide of Lucretia. Anchored to Lucretia + the assault by Tarquin's son; short verifiable answer supported verbatim ('se peremit'; cf. 1.19 'male sibi consciam se peremit'). Closed-book: one of the most celebrated suicides in Roman legend. Source_text normalization: OCR 'e peremit' corrected to 'se peremit' and 'uindicatam' to 'uindictam.'

author: Augustine
source_text: Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani, captiuus apud Carthaginienses fuit.
question: Apud quos captiuus fuit Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani?
question_en: Among whom was Marcus Regulus, a general of the Roman people, a captive?
derivation: Anchored to Marcus Regulus (named, 'imperator populi Romani'); single answer (the Carthaginians), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Regulus's captivity among the Carthaginians is a famous Roman exemplum.

author: Augustine
source_text: ad hoc impetrandum etiam istum praecipue Regulum cum legatis suis Romam miserunt, prius iuratione constrictum, si quod uolebant minime peregisset, rediturum esse Carthaginem. Perrexit ille atque in senatu contraria persuasit, quoniam non arbitrabatur utile esse Romanae rei publicae mutare captiuos. Nec post hanc persuasionem a suis ad hostes redire compulsus est, sed quia iurauerat, id sponte compleuit.
question: Quo Marcus Regulus, iureiurando constrictus, ex urbe Roma ad hostes sponte rediit?
question_en: To where did Marcus Regulus, bound by his oath, voluntarily return from the city of Rome to the enemy?
derivation: The celebrated Regulus exemplum: bound by oath, he voluntarily returned to the Carthaginians rather than break faith. Anchored to Regulus + the oath; single place answer (Carthaginem), supported verbatim ('rediturum esse Carthaginem'; 'quia iurauerat, id sponte compleuit'). Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: Sed tamen etiam illi praeter Lucretiam, de qua supra satis quod uidebatur diximus, non facile reperiunt de cuius auctoritate praescribant, nisi illum Catonem, qui se Vticae occidit.
question: Quo in loco Cato se ipse occidit, ut Augustinus commemorat?
question_en: In what place did Cato kill himself, as Augustine recounts?
derivation: Anchored to Cato (the younger, Cato Uticensis) by his suicide; single place answer (locative Vticae), supported verbatim ('qui se Vticae occidit'). Closed-book: Cato's suicide at Utica is among the most famous in Roman history.

author: Augustine
source_text: Cato enim numquam Caesarem uicerat, cui uictus dedignatus est subici et, ne subiceretur, a se ipso elegit occidi.
question: Cui uictori se subicere dedignatus Cato mortem sibi consciuit, ut Augustinus scribit?
question_en: To which victor did Cato disdain to submit, choosing instead to take his own life, as Augustine writes?
derivation: Anchored to Cato; single-name answer (dative Caesari), supported verbatim ('cui uictus dedignatus est subici et... a se ipso elegit occidi'). A distinct fact from the place of his death. Closed-book: Cato's refusal to live under Caesar's victory is famous.

author: Augustine
source_text: Egregius Romani nominis Marcus Marcellus, qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit, refertur eam prius fleuisse ruituram et ante eius sanguinem suas illi lacrimas effudisse.
question: Quam urbem Marcus Marcellus cepit, ut Augustinus refert?
question_en: Which city did Marcus Marcellus capture, as Augustine relates?
derivation: Anchored to Marcus Marcellus; single place-name answer (Syracusas), supported verbatim ('qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit'). Closed-book: Marcellus's capture of Syracuse (212 BC) is a well-known historical fact. 'ut Augustinus refert' mirrors the text's 'refertur.'

author: Augustine
source_text: Fabius, Tarentinae urbis euersor, a simulacrorum depraedatione se abstinuisse laudatur. Nam cum ei scriba suggessisset quid de signis deorum, quae multa capta fuerant, fieri iuberet, continentiam suam etiam iocando condiuit.
question: Cuius urbis euersor fuit ille Fabius qui se a deorum simulacrorum depraedatione abstinuisse laudatur?
question_en: Of what city was that Fabius the destroyer, who is praised for keeping himself from plundering the statues of the gods?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius via the detail that he abstained from plundering the gods' statues; single place answer (Tarentum), supported verbatim ('Tarentinae urbis euersor'). Closed-book: Fabius Maximus's recapture of Tarentum (209 BC) is historical.

author: Augustine
source_text: Romulus et Remus asylum constituisse perhibentur, quo quisquis confugeret ab omni noxa liber esset, augere quaerentes creandae multitudinem ciuitatis.
question: Qui asylum Romae constituisse perhibentur, quo confugientes ab omni noxa liberi essent, ut multitudinem ciuitatis augerent?
question_en: Who are said to have established an asylum at Rome, so that those fleeing to it would be free from all harm, in order to increase the city's population?
derivation: Anchored by the deed (founding the Roman asylum to enlarge the population); two-name answer (Romulus et Remus), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the asylum of Romulus is a standard part of Rome's foundation legend. 'perhibentur' kept to match the text's hedged attribution.

author: Augustine
source_text: qui tamen suis litteris credunt Arionem Methymnaeum, nobilissimum citharistam, cum esset deiectus e naui, exceptum delphini dorso et ad terras esse peruectum.
question: Quo animali Arion Methymnaeus, citharista nobilissimus, e naui deiectus ad terras peruectus esse fertur?
question_en: By what animal is Arion of Methymna, the renowned citharode, said to have been carried to land after being thrown from a ship?
derivation: Anchored to Arion of Methymna (named, 'nobilissimus citharista'); single answer (a dolphin, ablative Delphino), supported verbatim ('exceptum delphini dorso... ad terras esse peruectum'). Closed-book: the tale of Arion and the dolphin (Herodotus 1.23-24) is very famous. Augustine cites it as pagan lore ('suis litteris credunt'), hence 'fertur.'

author: Augustine
source_text: Vnde Paulinus noster, Nolensis episcopus, ex opulentissimo diuite uoluntate pauperrimus et copiosissime sanctus, quando et ipsam Nolam barbari uastauerunt, cum ab eis teneretur, sic in corde suo, ut ab eo postea cognouimus, precabatur.
question: Cuius urbis episcopus erat Paulinus, quem Augustinus, cum de barbarorum uastatione ageret, commemorat?
question_en: Of what city was Paulinus, whom Augustine mentions in connection with the barbarian devastation, the bishop?
derivation: Anchored to Paulinus ('Paulinus noster'); single place answer (Nola, the see of which he was bishop), supported verbatim ('Nolensis episcopus'). Closed-book: St. Paulinus of Nola is a well-known figure; Augustine reports his prayer when Nola too was sacked by the barbarians.

author: Augustine
source_text: illae quibus tenere cogebar Aeneae nescio cuius errores, oblitus errorum meorum, et plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore.
question: Cuius reginae mortem, quae se ab amore occidit, Augustinus puer in schola legens flebat?
question_en: Over which queen's death, who killed herself out of love, did the boy Augustine weep as he read in school?
derivation: The celebrated detail of Conf. 1: the boy wept over Dido's death ('plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore'). Anchored to Augustine + the named queen Dido; the question's description (a queen who killed herself for love) alone fixes the referent. Single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (one of the most-quoted episodes in the Confessions).

author: Augustine
source_text: illae quibus tenere cogebar Aeneae nescio cuius errores, oblitus errorum meorum, et plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore.
question: Cuius viri errores Augustinus puer in schola ediscere cogebatur?
question_en: Whose wanderings was the boy Augustine forced to learn by heart in school?
derivation: The wandering hero whose 'errores' Augustine was compelled to memorize is named in the text ('Aeneae nescio cuius errores'). Entity-anchored to Augustine's schooling + the named hero Aeneas; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book autobiographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: quid autem erat causae cur graecas litteras oderam, quibus puerulus imbuebar? ne nunc quidem mihi satis exploratum est. adamaveram enim latinas, non quas primi magistri sed quas docent qui grammatici vocantur.
question: Cum latinas litteras adamavisset, quas litteras Augustinus puer se odisse confitetur?
question_en: Although he had come to love Latin letters, which letters does Augustine confess he hated as a boy?
derivation: The well-known biographical fact that Augustine loved Latin but hated Greek as a schoolboy ('cur graecas litteras oderam ... adamaveram enim latinas'). Anchored to Augustine + the two named languages; clean which-language answer supported verbatim. Indirect statement 'se odisse' under 'confitetur'; concessive cum-clause with pluperfect subjunctive 'adamavisset'. Closed-book (Augustine's poor Greek is a standard fact about him).

author: Augustine
source_text: proponebatur enim mihi negotium, animae meae satis inquietum praemio laudis et dedecoris vel plagarum metu, ut dicerem verba Iunonis irascentis et dolentis quod non posset Italia Teucrorum avertere regem, quae numquam Iunonem dixisse audieram.
question: Cuius deae verba, irascentis et dolentis quod Teucrorum regem ab Italia avertere non posset, Augustino puero in schola dicenda proponebantur?
question_en: Whose words — those of a goddess angry and grieving that she could not turn the king of the Trojans away from Italy — was the boy Augustine set in school to declaim?
derivation: Augustine's school declamation exercise: putting into prose the angry speech of a goddess who could not keep the Trojan king from Italy ('verba Iunonis irascentis et dolentis quod non posset Italia Teucrorum avertere regem'). The description alone determines Juno (the Aeneid's divine antagonist), making it closed-book via both the Confessions and basic mythology. Single-name answer supported verbatim; anchored to Augustine's schooling + the named goddess and the Teucri/Italia.

author: Augustine
source_text: veni Carthaginem, et circumstrepebat me undique sartago flagitiosorum amorum.
question: In quam urbem Augustinus adulescens venit, ubi studiis eloquentiae operam dabat?
question_en: Into what city did the young Augustine come, where he was devoting himself to the study of eloquence?
derivation: The opening words of Book 3, 'veni Carthaginem.' Anchored to Augustine + his studies (he studies eloquence/rhetoric there, 3.3.6 'in schola rhetoris', 3.4.7 'discebam libros eloquentiae'); single place-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's student years at Carthage are a famous biographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: et usitato iam discendi ordine perveneram in librum cuiusdam Ciceronis, cuius linguam fere omnes mirantur, pectus non ita. sed liber ille ipsius exhortationem continet ad philosophiam et vocatur 'Hortensius'. ille vero liber mutavit affectum meum.
question: Quo titulo inscribitur liber Ciceronis quo lecto Augustinus ad amorem sapientiae accensus est?
question_en: Under what title is the book of Cicero, on reading which Augustine was kindled to the love of wisdom, inscribed?
derivation: Cicero's (now lost) Hortensius, an exhortation to philosophy, changed Augustine and inflamed him to wisdom ('liber ille ipsius exhortationem continet ad philosophiam et vocatur Hortensius. ille vero liber mutavit affectum meum'). Anchored to Cicero + Augustine; single title answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the most famous turning points in the Confessions.

author: Augustine
source_text: et usitato iam discendi ordine perveneram in librum cuiusdam Ciceronis, cuius linguam fere omnes mirantur, pectus non ita. sed liber ille ipsius exhortationem continet ad philosophiam et vocatur 'Hortensius'. ille vero liber mutavit affectum meum.
question: Cuius auctoris liber, exhortationem ad philosophiam continens, Augustinum ad sapientiae studium accendit?
question_en: Which author's book, containing an exhortation to philosophy, kindled Augustine to the pursuit of wisdom?
derivation: The book that inflamed Augustine to philosophy is by Cicero ('perveneram in librum cuiusdam Ciceronis... exhortationem continet ad philosophiam'). Anchored to Augustine + the Hortensius; single-name answer supported verbatim. Distinct fact (the author) from the work's title; closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: non enim ad acuendam linguam, quod videbar emere maternis mercedibus, cum agerem annum aetatis undevicensimum iam defuncto patre ante biennium, non ergo ad acuendam linguam referebam illum librum.
question: Quotum annum aetatis agebat Augustinus cum librum Ciceronis Hortensium legeret?
question_en: What year of his age was Augustine in when he read Cicero's book the Hortensius?
derivation: Number fact: Augustine read the Hortensius in the nineteenth year of his age ('cum agerem annum aetatis undevicensimum'). Anchored to Augustine + the reading of the Hortensius; short, verifiable answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: et credidi miser magis esse misericordiam praestandam fructibus terrae quam hominibus propter quos nascerentur. si quis enim esuriens peteret qui manichaeus non esset, quasi capitali supplicio damnanda buccella videretur si ei daretur.
question: Cuius haereticae sectae asseclam se Augustinus adulescens per plures annos fuisse confitetur?
question_en: Of what heretical sect does Augustine confess that he was a follower for several years as a young man?
derivation: Augustine names the Manichees while describing his own former belief that food should be given only to a Manichee ('si quis... qui manichaeus non esset...'); the Manichee period dominates the latter half of Book 3. Anchored to Augustine; single-name answer supported by 'manichaeus'. Closed-book: Augustine's years as a Manichee are among the most famous facts of his life. (Indirect statement 'se... asseclam fuisse' governed by 'confitetur'.)

author: Augustine
source_text: nam novem ferme anni secuti sunt quibus ego in illo limo profundi ac tenebris falsitatis, cum saepe surgere conarer et gravius alliderer, volutatus sum.
question: Per quot fere annos Augustinus in errore Manichaeorum versatus est?
question_en: For about how many years was Augustine entangled in the error of the Manichees?
derivation: Number fact: 'novem ferme anni secuti sunt' in which Augustine was mired in falsity — the Manichee error that is the subject of Book 3. Answer mirrors the approximative 'ferme'. Anchored to Augustine + the Manichees; short, verifiable. Closed-book: the roughly nine years as a Manichee are a famous biographical datum.

author: Augustine
source_text: vidit enim se stantem in quadam regula lignea et advenientem ad se iuvenem splendidum hilarem atque arridentem sibi, cum illa esset maerens et maerore confecta.
question: In qua re Monica, mater Augustini, se stantem per somnium vidit, cum iuvenis splendidus ad eam accederet?
question_en: On what did Monica, Augustine's mother, see herself standing in a dream, as a radiant young man approached her?
derivation: Monica's famous consolatory dream: she sees herself standing on a wooden rule ('se stantem in quadam regula lignea') when a radiant youth tells her that where she is, there her son will also be. Anchored to Monica (Augustine's mother, well known though unnamed in this book) + the dream; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the dream of Monica is a celebrated episode.

author: Augustine
source_text: ille iam substomachans taedio, 'vade' inquit 'a me. ita vivas: fieri non potest, ut filius istarum lacrimarum pereat.'
question: Quibus verbis episcopus quidam Monicam, Augustini matrem, de filii salute consolatus est?
answer: Fieri non potest, ut filius istarum lacrimarum pereat.
question_en: With what words did a certain bishop console Monica, Augustine's mother, concerning her son's salvation?
answer_en: It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.
derivation: The famous consoling saying of the (unnamed) bishop to the weeping Monica. Anchored to Monica (Augustine's mother) + the bishop; the answer is the famous quoted sentence supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of the Confessions. Kept as a short famous quotation per the task; the bishop himself is unnamed in the text ('quendam episcopum').

author: Augustine
source_text: per idem tempus annorum novem, ab undevicensimo anno aetatis meae usque ad duodetricensimum, seducebamur et seducebamus, falsi atque fallentes in variis cupiditatibus.
question: A quoto aetatis suae anno usque ad quotum illud novem annorum tempus pertinuisse Augustinus confitetur, quo et deceptus est et decepit?
question_en: From which year of his age to which does Augustine confess that period of nine years extended, in which he was both deceived and deceived others?
answer_en: From his nineteenth to his twenty-eighth.
derivation: Augustine dates his nine-year period of error precisely: 'annorum novem, ab undevicensimo anno aetatis meae usque ad duodetricensimum' (from his 19th to his 28th year). Number/span fact anchored to Augustine + the nine years he was 'falsi atque fallentes' (a Manichee hearer). Indirect statement (tempus pertinuisse) under confitetur; relative clause mirrors 'seducebamur et seducebamus.' Closed-book: his roughly nine years as a Manichee, ages 19-28, is standard biography (cf. conf5 'per annos ferme novem').

author: Augustine
source_text: docebam in illis annis artem rhetoricam, et victoriosam loquacitatem victus cupiditate vendebam.
question: Quam artem liberalem Augustinus iuvenis, antequam ad fidem catholicam converteretur, docebat?
question_en: What liberal art did the young Augustine teach, before he was converted to the catholic faith?
derivation: Augustine states he taught rhetoric in these years: 'docebam in illis annis artem rhetoricam.' Anchored to Augustine + his pre-conversion years; short answer (rhetoric), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's career as a teacher of rhetoric is among the best-known facts of his life.

author: Augustine
source_text: erat eo tempore vir sagax, medicinae artis peritissimus atque in ea nobilissimus, qui proconsul manu sua coronam illam agonisticam imposuerat non sano capiti meo, sed non ut medicus.
question: Qua in arte nobilissimus erat ille proconsul qui coronam agonisticam capiti Augustini manu sua imposuit?
question_en: In what art was that proconsul most distinguished, who with his own hand placed the contest-crown on Augustine's head?
derivation: The proconsul who crowned Augustine at the poetic contest is identified as a physician of the first rank: 'vir sagax, medicinae artis peritissimus atque in ea nobilissimus, qui proconsul... coronam illam agonisticam imposuerat... capiti meo.' Anchored to that proconsul + Augustine; short answer (medicine), supported verbatim. NB: Book 4 does NOT name him; this is the physician-proconsul (Vindicianus, named only later, at Conf. 7.6.8) who in this same section urges Augustine to abandon astrology ('monuit ut eos abicerem') -- so the answer is his profession, which the text states, not a name the text withholds.

author: Augustine
source_text: et tamen fugi de patria. minus enim eum quaerebant oculi mei ubi videre non solebant, atque a Thagastensi oppido veni Carthaginem.
question: Quo Augustinus ex oppido Thagastensi, post mortem amici carissimi maerens, se contulit?
question_en: Where did Augustine betake himself from the town of Thagaste, grieving after the death of his dearest friend?
derivation: Fleeing his homeland after his friend's death, Augustine went from Thagaste to Carthage: 'a Thagastensi oppido veni Carthaginem.' Anchored to Augustine + Thagaste + the friend's death; single place answer (Carthage), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's origin at Thagaste and his move to Carthage are canonical biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: et ista consideratio scaturrivit in animo meo ex intimo corde meo, et scripsi libros 'de pulchro et apto' — puto duos aut tres: tu scis, deus, nam excidit mihi.
question: Quo titulo inscripsit Augustinus primum illud opus quod, de pulchritudine disputans, composuit?
question_en: Under what title did Augustine entitle that first work which he composed, discoursing on beauty?
answer_en: On the Beautiful and the Fitting (De pulchro et apto).
derivation: Augustine's earliest composition is named in the text: 'scripsi libros de pulchro et apto.' Anchored to Augustine + his first work on beauty; short title answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book: De pulchro et apto is universally cited as Augustine's first (now lost) book.

author: Augustine
source_text: quid est autem quod me movit, domine deus meus, ut ad Hierium, Romanae urbis oratorem, scriberem illos libros? quem non noveram facie, sed amaveram hominem ex doctrinae fama, quae illi clara erat.
question: Ad quem virum Augustinus libros suos 'de pulchro et apto' scripsit?
question_en: To which man did Augustine address his books 'On the Beautiful and the Fitting'?
derivation: Augustine addressed his De pulchro et apto to Hierius: 'ut ad Hierium... scriberem illos libros.' Anchored to Augustine + the named work; single-name answer (Hierius), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the dedication of Augustine's first book to the orator Hierius is the standard biographical detail, though Augustine had never met him face to face ('quem non noveram facie').

author: Augustine
source_text: quid est autem quod me movit, domine deus meus, ut ad Hierium, Romanae urbis oratorem, scriberem illos libros?
question: Cuius urbis orator erat Hierius, ad quem Augustinus libros 'de pulchro et apto' misit?
question_en: Of what city was Hierius, to whom Augustine sent his books 'On the Beautiful and the Fitting,' an orator?
derivation: Hierius is identified as an orator of Rome: 'ad Hierium, Romanae urbis oratorem.' Anchored to Hierius (named) + the dedication of Augustine's work; single place answer (Rome), supported verbatim. Distinct from the dedication-name fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: et eram aetate annorum fortasse viginti sex aut septem, cum illa volumina scripsi, volvens apud me corporalia figmenta obstrepentia cordis mei auribus, quas intendebam, dulcis veritas, in interiorem melodiam tuam, cogitans de pulchro et apto.
question: Quot fere annos natus erat Augustinus cum illa volumina 'de pulchro et apto' conscripsit?
question_en: About how many years old was Augustine when he wrote those volumes 'On the Beautiful and the Fitting'?
derivation: Augustine gives his age when he wrote the De pulchro et apto: 'eram aetate annorum fortasse viginti sex aut septem, cum illa volumina scripsi... cogitans de pulchro et apto.' Number fact anchored to Augustine + the named work; the answer mirrors his own 'fortasse' (perhaps 26 or 27), supported verbatim.

author: Augustine
source_text: et quid mihi proderat quod annos natus ferme viginti, cum in manus meas venissent aristotelica quaedam, quas appellant decem categorias (quarum nomine, cum eas rhetor Carthaginiensis, magister meus, buccis typho crepantibus commemoraret et alii qui docti habebantur, tamquam in nescio quid magnum et divinum suspensus inhiabam), legi eas solus et intellexi?
question: Cuius philosophi opus, quod 'decem categorias' appellant, Augustinus adulescens legit et per se intellexit?
question_en: Whose work, which they call the 'Ten Categories,' did the young Augustine read and understand by himself?
derivation: The 'ten categories' Augustine read are Aristotle's: 'aristotelica quaedam, quas appellant decem categorias.' Anchored to the work (the Categoriae) + Augustine; single-name answer (Aristotle), supported verbatim. Closed-book: that Augustine read Aristotle's Categories as a young man is a standard fact of his intellectual biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: et quid mihi proderat quod annos natus ferme viginti, cum in manus meas venissent aristotelica quaedam, quas appellant decem categorias (quarum nomine, cum eas rhetor Carthaginiensis, magister meus, buccis typho crepantibus commemoraret et alii qui docti habebantur, tamquam in nescio quid magnum et divinum suspensus inhiabam), legi eas solus et intellexi?
question: Aristotelis decem categorias Augustinus utrum magistro tradente an nullo docente intellexit?
question_en: Did Augustine understand Aristotle's Ten Categories with a teacher's instruction, or with no one teaching him?
answer_en: By himself, with no one teaching him.
derivation: Augustine stresses that he read and grasped Aristotle's Categories unaided: 'legi eas solus et intellexi'; others who had needed eminent teachers could tell him no more than he had worked out alone. Anchored to Augustine + Aristotle's Categories; short answer (alone/unaided), supported verbatim by 'solus.' Closed-book: his effortless solo reading of the Categories is a celebrated detail of the Confessions.

author: Augustine
source_text: iam venerat Carthaginem quidam manichaeorum episcopus, Faustus nomine, magnus laqueus diaboli, et multi implicabantur in eo per inlecebram suaviloquentiae.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur ille Manichaeorum episcopus qui Carthaginem venit, quem Augustinus diu venturum expectabat?
question_en: By what name was that Manichaean bishop who came to Carthage, whom Augustine long awaited, called?
derivation: The Manichee bishop whose arrival at Carthage dominates Book 5 is named verbatim: 'manichaeorum episcopus, Faustus nomine.' Anchored to the Manichees + Carthage + Augustine's long expectation; single-name answer. Closed-book: Faustus is famous (Augustine later wrote Contra Faustum Manichaeum).

author: Augustine
source_text: iam venerat Carthaginem quidam manichaeorum episcopus, Faustus nomine, magnus laqueus diaboli.
question: Cuius sectae episcopus erat Faustus, quem Augustinus Carthagini audivit?
question_en: Of what sect was Faustus, whom Augustine heard at Carthage, a bishop?
derivation: Faustus is identified as a bishop of the Manichees ('manichaeorum episcopus, Faustus nomine'). Anchored to Faustus by name; single-answer (the sect/office), distinct from the name fact. Closed-book biographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: proloquar in conspectu dei mei annum illum undetricensimum aetatis meae. iam venerat Carthaginem quidam manichaeorum episcopus, Faustus nomine, magnus laqueus diaboli.
question: Quoto anno aetatis suae Augustinus Faustum Carthaginem venisse narrat?
question_en: In which year of his age does Augustine relate that Faustus came to Carthage?
derivation: Augustine opens by declaring the year he is narrating, his 29th ('annum illum undetricensimum aetatis meae'), in which Faustus had come to Carthage. Number fact anchored to Augustine + Faustus's arrival; undetricensimus = 29th. Short, verifiable; age facts are precedent (cf. conf9).

author: Augustine
source_text: et per annos ferme ipsos novem quibus eos animo vagabundus audivi nimis extento desiderio venturum expectabam istum Faustum.
question: Per quot fere annos Augustinus Manichaeos audiverat, dum Faustum venturum expectabat?
question_en: For about how many years had Augustine been listening to the Manichees while he awaited the coming of Faustus?
derivation: Number fact: Augustine had heard the Manichees for about nine years, awaiting Faustus ('per annos ferme ipsos novem... audivi... expectabam istum Faustum'). Answer mirrors the approximative 'ferme.' Anchored to Augustine + Manichees + Faustus. Closed-book: his ~9 years as a Manichaean auditor is standard biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: egisti ergo mecum ut mihi persuaderetur Romam pergere et potius ibi docere quod docebam Carthagini.
question: Quo Augustinus ex Carthagine docendi causa transiit?
question_en: Where did Augustine cross over to from Carthage for the sake of teaching?
derivation: Augustine was persuaded to leave Carthage (where he taught) and go to Rome to teach there ('Romam pergere et potius ibi docere quod docebam Carthagini'). Anchored to Augustine + Carthage; single place answer. Closed-book: his move from Carthage to Rome is canonical biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: et ecce excipior ibi flagello aegritudinis corporalis, et ibam iam ad inferos portans omnia mala quae commiseram et in te et in me et in alios.
question: In qua urbe Augustinus, mox ut eo ex Africa pervenit, gravi corporis aegritudine correptus est?
question_en: In what city was Augustine struck down by a grave bodily illness soon after he arrived there from Africa?
derivation: On reaching Rome from Africa, Augustine was seized by bodily illness ('excipior ibi flagello aegritudinis corporalis'; the 'ibi' is Rome, where he had just sailed from Carthage). Anchored to Augustine + Rome + arrival from Africa; single place answer. Closed-book: his near-fatal illness at Rome is a known episode.

author: Augustine
source_text: itaque posteaquam missum est a Mediolanio Romam ad praefectum urbis, ut illi civitati rhetoricae magister provideretur, impertita etiam evectione publica, ego ipse ambivi per eos ipsos manichaeis vanitatibus ebrios (quibus ut carerem ibam, sed utrique nesciebamus) ut dictione proposita me probatum praefectus tunc Symmachus mitteret.
question: Quis praefectus urbis Augustinum Mediolanium misit, ut illic rhetoricam doceret?
question_en: Which prefect of the City sent Augustine to Milan to teach rhetoric there?
derivation: The prefect of Rome, Symmachus, having approved Augustine by a set declamation, sent him to Milan ('praefectus tunc Symmachus mitteret'). Anchored to the prefecture of Rome + Milan + Augustine; single-name answer. Closed-book: Q. Aurelius Symmachus is a well-known figure.

author: Augustine
source_text: itaque posteaquam missum est a Mediolanio Romam ad praefectum urbis, ut illi civitati rhetoricae magister provideretur, impertita etiam evectione publica, ego ipse ambivi per eos ipsos manichaeis vanitatibus ebrios (quibus ut carerem ibam, sed utrique nesciebamus) ut dictione proposita me probatum praefectus tunc Symmachus mitteret. et veni Mediolanium ad Ambrosium episcopum, in optimis notum orbi terrae, pium cultorem tuum.
question: Quo Augustinus, a Symmacho praefecto probatus, rhetoricae magister missus est?
question_en: Where was Augustine sent as a teacher of rhetoric after being approved by the prefect Symmachus?
derivation: Milan had asked Rome's prefect to provide it a teacher of rhetoric ('a Mediolanio... ut illi civitati rhetoricae magister provideretur'); Symmachus sent Augustine, who 'veni Mediolanium.' Anchored to Augustine + Symmachus + the office of rhetoric-master; single place answer (Mediolanium). Closed-book: his professorship at Milan is standard biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: et veni Mediolanium ad Ambrosium episcopum, in optimis notum orbi terrae, pium cultorem tuum, cuius tunc eloquia strenue ministrabant adipem frumenti tui et laetitiam olei et sobriam vini ebrietatem populo tuo.
question: Ad quem episcopum Augustinus Mediolanium veniens accessit?
question_en: To which bishop did Augustine come on arriving at Milan?
derivation: On reaching Milan Augustine came to its bishop Ambrose ('et veni Mediolanium ad Ambrosium episcopum'). Anchored to Augustine + Milan; single-name answer. Closed-book: Ambrose of Milan and his role in Augustine's conversion are famous.

author: Augustine
source_text: et studiose audiebam disputantem in populo, non intentione qua debui, sed quasi explorans eius facundiam, utrum conveniret famae suae an maior minorve proflueret quam praedicabatur.
question: Quid potissimum in Ambrosio Augustinus primo explorabat, cum eum in populo disputantem audiret?
question_en: What above all did Augustine at first examine in Ambrose when he heard him preaching to the people?
derivation: Augustine eagerly listened to Ambrose preaching to the people, at first attending to his eloquence rather than the content ('quasi explorans eius facundiam'; 'rerum autem incuriosus'). Anchored to Augustine + Ambrose; short answer (his eloquence/facundia) supported verbatim. Fact-seeking and closed-book: the well-known point that Augustine first came for Ambrose's rhetoric.

author: Augustine
source_text: iam venerat ad me mater pietate fortis, terra marique me sequens et in periculis omnibus de te secura.
question: Quomodo mater Augustini eum secuta est?
question_en: How did Augustine's mother follow him?
derivation: Opening of Book 6: Augustine's mother had come to him (at Milan), following him over land and sea ('terra marique me sequens'). Anchored to Augustine + his mother; short adverbial answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Monica's crossing the sea to join Augustine in Italy is a standard fact of his biography. NOTE: Monica is not named in Book 6 (only 'mater'); the pair relies on her being universally known as Augustine's mother.

author: Augustine
source_text: et invenit me, periclitantem quidem graviter desperatione indagandae veritatis, sed tamen ei cum indicassem non me quidem iam esse manichaeum, sed neque catholicum christianum, non quasi inopinatum aliquid audierit, exilivit laetitia.
question: Quid se iam non esse Augustinus matri suae indicavit, cum eum illa invenisset?
question_en: What did Augustine indicate to his mother that he no longer was, when she had found him?
derivation: When his mother reached him she found he was no longer a Manichee, though not yet a Catholic Christian ('non me quidem iam esse manichaeum, sed neque catholicum christianum'). Anchored to Augustine + his mother; single-word answer supported verbatim by 'manichaeum'. Closed-book (Augustine's break with Manichaeism is a famous turning point). NOTE: 'mater' = Monica, not named in this book.

author: Augustine
source_text: sed cum legebat, oculi ducebantur per paginas et cor intellectum rimabatur, vox autem et lingua quiescebant.
question: Quomodo legere solebat Ambrosius, cum eum Augustinus observaret?
question_en: How did Ambrose use to read, when Augustine observed him?
derivation: The famous report of Ambrose reading silently: eyes ran over the page while 'vox autem et lingua quiescebant' (further on: 'sic eum legentem vidimus tacite'). Anchored to Ambrose (subject of the surrounding passage, named at the start of 6.3.3 as 'ipsumque Ambrosium') + Augustine the observer; short answer. Closed-book: often cited as the locus classicus for silent reading in antiquity.

author: Augustine
source_text: non sane relinquens incantatam sibi a parentibus terrenam viam, Romam praecesserat ut ius disceret, et ibi gladiatorii spectaculi hiatu incredibili et incredibiliter abreptus est.
question: Quid Alypius Romam profectus discere voluit?
question_en: What did Alypius set out for Rome to learn?
derivation: Alypius went ahead to Rome to study law ('Romam praecesserat ut ius disceret'). Anchored to Alypius + Rome; single-word answer supported verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact about Augustine's well-known friend.

author: Augustine
source_text: non sane relinquens incantatam sibi a parentibus terrenam viam, Romam praecesserat ut ius disceret, et ibi gladiatorii spectaculi hiatu incredibili et incredibiliter abreptus est.
question: Quo genere spectaculi Alypius Romae victus atque abreptus est?
question_en: By what kind of spectacle was Alypius overcome and carried away at Rome?
derivation: The celebrated episode: dragged to the amphitheatre, Alypius was overcome by the gladiatorial games ('gladiatorii spectaculi hiatu incredibili... abreptus est'). Anchored to Alypius + Rome; short noun-phrase answer supported verbatim. One of the most famous episodes of the Confessions, hence closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: Nebridius etiam, qui relicta patria vicina Carthagini atque ipsa Carthagine, ubi frequentissimus erat, relicto paterno rure optimo, relicta domo et non secutura matre, nullam ob aliam causam Mediolanium venerat, nisi ut mecum viveret in flagrantissimo studio veritatis atque sapientiae.
question: Quam ad urbem Nebridius venit, ut una cum Augustino studio sapientiae operam daret?
question_en: To what city did Nebridius come, in order to pursue the study of wisdom together with Augustine?
derivation: Nebridius left his homeland and came to Milan for no other reason than to live with Augustine in the ardent pursuit of truth and wisdom ('Mediolanium venerat, nisi ut mecum viveret in flagrantissimo studio veritatis atque sapientiae'). Anchored to Nebridius + Augustine; single place-name answer (acc. of motion-toward) supported verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: et ego maxime mirabar, satagens et recolens quam longum tempus esset ab undevicensimo anno aetatis meae, quo fervere coeperam studio sapientiae, disponens ea inventa relinquere omnes vanarum cupiditatum spes inanes et insanias mendaces.
question: Quoto anno aetatis suae Augustinus studio sapientiae fervere coepisse se dicit?
question_en: In which year of his life does Augustine say he began to burn with zeal for the study of wisdom?
