derivation: Number fact anchored to Augustine: he began to burn with zeal for wisdom from his nineteenth year ('ab undevicensimo anno aetatis meae, quo fervere coeperam studio sapientiae'), i.e. the awakening by Cicero's Hortensius (cf. Book 3). Indirect statement 'coepisse se dicit'; short ordinal answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: interea mea peccata multiplicabantur, et avulsa a latere meo tamquam impedimento coniugii cum qua cubare solitus eram, cor, ubi adhaerebat, concisum et vulneratum mihi erat et trahebat sanguinem. et illa in Africam redierat, vovens tibi alium se virum nescituram, relicto apud me naturali ex illa filio meo.
question: Quo terrarum rediit femina quacum Augustinus cubare solebat, relicto apud eum filio naturali?
question_en: To what region did the woman with whom Augustine used to sleep return, leaving his natural son behind with him?
derivation: Augustine's long-time concubine, the mother of his son, was torn from his side and returned to Africa, leaving his natural son with him ('et illa in Africam redierat... relicto apud me naturali ex illa filio meo'). Anchored to Augustine + his concubine + their son; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a famous episode of the Confessions.

author: Augustine
source_text: procurasti mihi per quendam hominem immanissimo typho turgidum quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos.
question: Cuius sectae philosophorum libros, ex graeca lingua in latinam versos, homo quidam immani superbia turgidus Augustino legendos procuravit?
question_en: The books of which sect of philosophers, translated from Greek into Latin, did a certain man swollen with monstrous pride procure for Augustine to read?
derivation: The pivotal moment of Book 7: a man 'swollen with monstrous pride' provides Augustine certain books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin ('quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos'). Anchored to Augustine + the proud benefactor; single answer (Platonicorum), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the 'libri Platonicorum' that turned Augustine toward an incorporeal God are a famous landmark of his biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: procurasti mihi per quendam hominem immanissimo typho turgidum quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos.
question: Ex qua lingua in quam linguam versi erant illi platonicorum libri quos Augustinus legit?
question_en: From what language into what language had those books of the Platonists which Augustine read been translated?
derivation: Distinct fact from the same sentence: the Platonist books Augustine read were Latin translations from Greek ('ex graeca lingua in latinam versos'). Anchored to the libri Platonicorum; short, verifiable, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's reliance on Latin versions of the Platonists (he had little Greek) is a noted detail of his intellectual formation.

author: Augustine
source_text: tu procurasti pervicaciae meae, qua obluctatus sum Vindiciano acuto seni et Nebridio adulescenti mirabilis animae, illi vehementer adfirmanti, huic cum dubitatione quidem aliqua sed tamen crebro dicenti non esse illam artem futura praevidendi.
question: Qui duo, senex acutus et adulescens mirabilis animae, Augustino adfirmabant non esse veram illam artem futura praevidendi?
question_en: Which two men, a shrewd old man and a young man of marvelous soul, affirmed to Augustine that the art of foretelling the future was not real?
derivation: Two named figures dissuaded Augustine from astrology: Vindicianus, the shrewd old man (vehemently), and Nebridius, the young man (with some hesitation) -- both saying 'non esse illam artem futura praevidendi.' Anchored to Augustine + the astrology question; the senex/adulescens descriptors mirror 'acuto seni' / 'adulescenti.' Two named answers, both required, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's rejection of astrology under Vindicianus and Nebridius is standard biography.

author: Augustine
source_text: is ergo vir nomine Firminus, liberaliter institutus et excultus eloquio, cum me tamquam carissimum de quibusdam suis rebus, in quas saecularis spes eius intumuerat, consuleret, quid mihi secundum suas quas constellationes appellant videretur.
question: Quod erat nomen illius viri liberaliter instituti qui Augustinum, de astrologia iam dubitantem, de constellationibus suis consuluit?
question_en: What was the name of that liberally educated man who, when Augustine was already in doubt about astrology, consulted him about his horoscope (constellationes)?
derivation: The man whose case clinched Augustine's rejection of astrology is named: 'is ergo vir nomine Firminus, liberaliter institutus,' who consulted Augustine about his 'constellationes.' Anchored to Augustine + the astrology consultation; single-name answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Firminus is the named protagonist of the famous twin-birth anecdote in Confessions 7.

author: Augustine
source_text: et non erunt vera, quia easdem litteras inspiciens eadem debuit dicere de Esau et de Iacob, sed non eadem utrique acciderunt. falsa ergo diceret aut, si vera diceret, non eadem diceret: at eadem inspiceret.
question: Quos geminos, eodem tempore natos sed non eadem fortuna usos, Augustinus contra astrologorum artem in exemplum adduxit?
question_en: Which twins, born at the same time but not enjoying the same fortune, did Augustine adduce as an example against the art of the astrologers?
derivation: Against astrology Augustine adduces the scriptural twins Esau and Jacob: one horoscope ('easdem litteras') ought to have predicted the same for both, yet 'non eadem utrique acciderunt.' Anchored to Augustine's argument against astrologers + the named twins; single answer (Esau et Iacob), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Esau and Jacob as twins of divergent fortune are universally known.

author: Augustine
source_text: itaque avidissime arripui venerabilem stilum spiritus tui, et prae ceteris apostolum Paulum.
question: Quem apostolum Augustinus, lectis platonicorum libris, prae ceteris avidissime arripuit?
question_en: Which apostle did Augustine, after reading the books of the Platonists, eagerly take up above the rest?
derivation: After the Platonist books Augustine turns to Scripture and above all to Paul ('prae ceteris apostolum Paulum'). Anchored to Augustine + the sequence after the libri Platonicorum; single-name answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book: that Augustine moved from the Platonists to the epistles of Paul is a canonical step in his conversion narrative.

author: Augustine
source_text: Alypius autem deum carne indutum ita putabat credi a catholicis ut praeter deum et carnem non esset in Christo, animam mentemque hominis non existimabat in eo praedicari. et quoniam bene persuasum tenebat ea quae de illo memoriae mandata sunt sine vitali et rationali creatura non fieri, ad ipsam christianam fidem pigrius movebatur. sed postea haereticorum apollinaristarum hunc errorem esse cognoscens catholicae fidei conlaetatus et contemperatus est.
question: Quorum haereticorum errorem hunc esse Alypius postea cognovit, qui animam mentemque hominis in Christo praedicari non existimaverat?
question_en: Of which heretics did Alypius later recognize this to be the error, he who had not thought that a human soul and mind were proclaimed in Christ?
derivation: Alypius had thought Christ was God clothed in flesh without a human soul and mind, an opinion he later recognized to be 'haereticorum apollinaristarum hunc errorem.' Anchored to Alypius + his christological view; single named answer (the Apollinarists), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Apollinarian heresy (denying Christ a human soul) is a known doctrinal label, here attached by Augustine to Alypius.

author: Augustine
source_text: ubi autem commemoravi legisse me quosdam libros platonicorum, quos Victorinus, quondam rhetor urbis Romae, quem christianum defunctum esse audieram, in latinam linguam transtulisset, gratulatus est mihi quod non in aliorum philosophorum scripta incidissem plena fallaciarum et deceptionum secundum elementa huius mundi.
question: Quis libros platonicorum, quos Augustinus legerat, in latinam linguam transtulit?
question_en: Who translated into Latin the books of the Platonists that Augustine had read?
derivation: Augustine recounts to Simplicianus that he had read certain Platonist books which Victorinus, once a rhetor of the city of Rome, had translated into Latin. Anchored to the libri platonicorum + Latin; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'quos Victorinus ... in latinam linguam transtulisset.' Closed-book: Marius Victorinus's Latin renderings of the Neoplatonists are a well-known fact of intellectual history.

author: Augustine
source_text: doctor tot nobilium senatorum, qui etiam ob insigne praeclari magisterii, quod cives huius mundi eximium putant, statuam Romano foro meruerat et acceperat.
question: In quo loco Victorinus rhetor, ob praeclarum magisterium, statuam meruit et accepit?
question_en: In what place did Victorinus the rhetor earn and receive a statue, on account of his distinguished teaching?
derivation: Victorinus, teacher of many noble senators, earned and received a statue in the Roman forum for his eminent teaching of rhetoric. Anchored to Victorinus the rhetor; place answer supported verbatim by 'statuam Romano foro meruerat et acceperat.' Closed-book biographical detail (his statue in the forum is a famous mark of his standing as rhetor at Rome).

author: Augustine
source_text: sed ubi mihi homo tuus Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit, exarsi ad imitandum: ad hoc enim et ille narraverat.
question: Quis Augustino de conversione Victorini rhetoris narravit?
question_en: Who recounted to Augustine the conversion of Victorinus the rhetor?
derivation: It was Simplicianus who told Augustine the story of Victorinus's conversion, precisely to spur him to imitate it. Anchored to Augustine + Victorinus; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit.' Closed-book (Simplicianus, later bishop of Milan, is a recognized figure in the conversion narrative).

author: Augustine
source_text: posteaquam vero et illud addidit, quod imperatoris Iuliani temporibus lege data prohibiti sunt christiani docere litteraturam et oratoriam. quam legem ille amplexus, loquacem scholam deserere maluit.
question: Cuius imperatoris temporibus christiani lege data docere litteraturam et oratoriam prohibiti sunt?
question_en: In which emperor's reign were Christians forbidden by a law to teach literature and rhetoric?
derivation: Augustine reports that under the emperor Julian a law forbade Christians to teach literature and rhetoric, a law Victorinus embraced by leaving his school. Anchored to the school-teaching ban; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'imperatoris Iuliani temporibus lege data prohibiti sunt christiani docere litteraturam et oratoriam.' Closed-book (Julian's edict on teachers, AD 362, is established Roman history).

author: Augustine
source_text: cui ego cum indicassem illis me scripturis curam maximam impendere, ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio Aegyptio monacho, cuius nomen excellenter clarebat apud servos tuos, nos autem usque in illam horam latebat.
question: Quis, cum in domum Augustini et Alypii venisset, eis de Antonio Aegyptio monacho narravit?
question_en: Who, having come to the house of Augustine and Alypius, told them about Antony the Egyptian monk?
derivation: The teller ('ipso narrante') is Ponticianus, named at the opening of 8.6.14 ('ad nos domum venit ad me et Alypium Ponticianus quidam ... praeclare in palatio militans'). Anchored to Augustine + Alypius + Antony; single-name answer. Closed-book: Ponticianus's visit is the famous trigger of Augustine's conversion.

author: Augustine
source_text: ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio Aegyptio monacho, cuius nomen excellenter clarebat apud servos tuos, nos autem usque in illam horam latebat.
question: Quo nomine appellatur monachus Aegyptius de quo Ponticianus apud Augustinum narravit?
question_en: By what name is the Egyptian monk called about whom Ponticianus spoke at Augustine's house?
derivation: Ponticianus's conversation turned to Antony, the Egyptian monk. Anchored to Ponticianus + Egyptian monk; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'de Antonio Aegyptio monacho.' Closed-book (Antony of Egypt is among the most famous of the early monks).

author: Augustine
source_text: sed illos vagabundos inruisse in quandam casam ubi habitabant quidam servi tui spiritu pauperes, qualium est regnum caelorum, et invenisse ibi codicem in quo scripta erat vita Antonii. quam legere coepit unus eorum et mirari et accendi, et inter legendum meditari arripere talem vitam et relicta militia saeculari servire tibi. erant autem ex eis quos dicunt agentes in rebus.
question: Cuius vita scripta erat in codice quem agentes in rebus, Ponticiani contubernales, reppererunt, quo lecto militiam saecularem reliquerunt?
question_en: Whose life was written in the codex that the agentes in rebus, Ponticianus's companions, found, and which, once read, made them abandon their worldly service?
derivation: Two of Ponticianus's fellow court officials ('agentes in rebus') found in a cottage a codex containing the Life of Antony, and reading it abandoned their imperial careers. Anchored to the officials + the codex; answer supported verbatim by 'codicem in quo scripta erat vita Antonii.' Closed-book (the role of Athanasius's Vita Antonii in these conversions is a famous episode).

author: Augustine
source_text: et ecce audio vocem de vicina domo cum cantu dicentis et crebro repetentis, quasi pueri an puellae, nescio: 'tolle lege, tolle lege.'
question: Quae verba Augustinus, in horto sedens, a voce quasi pueri vel puellae de vicina domo crebro repeti audivit?
question_en: What words did Augustine, sitting in the garden, hear repeated again and again by a voice as of a boy or girl from a neighboring house?
derivation: The famous chant that prompted Augustine to open the apostle's codex. Anchored to Augustine + the garden scene; the quoted words are supported verbatim by "'tolle lege, tolle lege.'" Closed-book (one of the most famous moments in the Confessions) and translatable ('take up and read').

author: Augustine
source_text: et forte supra mensam lusoriam quae ante nos erat attendit codicem. tulit, aperuit, invenit apostolum Paulum, inopinate sane: putaverat enim aliquid de libris quorum professio me conterebat.
question: Cuius apostoli scripta continebat codex, quem Ponticianus in domo Augustini aperuit et quem Augustinus postea in horto arripuit ac legit?
question_en: Whose apostolic writings did the codex contain, which Ponticianus opened in Augustine's house and which Augustine afterward seized and read in the garden?
derivation: The codex on the gaming table that Ponticianus opened proved to contain 'apostolum Paulum'; it is the same 'codicem apostoli' Augustine seized and read at his conversion (8.12.29, Rom. 13:13-14). Anchored to Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'invenit apostolum Paulum.' Closed-book (Augustine's conversion reading of Paul is famous).

author: Augustine
source_text: itaque concitus redii in eum locum ubi sedebat Alypius: ibi enim posueram codicem apostoli cum inde surrexeram. arripui, aperui, et legi in silentio capitulum quo primum coniecti sunt oculi mei.
question: Quis amicus una cum Augustino in horto sedebat quo tempore, codice apostoli arripto, ad fidem conversus est?
question_en: Which friend was sitting with Augustine in the garden at the time when, having seized the apostle's codex, he was converted to the faith?
derivation: Alypius was beside Augustine throughout the garden scene ('Alypius affixus lateri meo' 8.11.27; 'ubi sedebat Alypius' 8.12.29; 'indicavi Alypio' 8.12.30) and converted with him. Anchored to Augustine + the garden conversion; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'redii in eum locum ubi sedebat Alypius.' Closed-book (Alypius is Augustine's well-known companion).

author: Augustine
source_text: pariter remeabamus in Africam. et cum apud Ostia Tiberina essemus, mater defuncta est.
question: In quo loco mater Augustini mortua est, cum in Africam redire pararent?
question_en: In what place did Augustine's mother die, as they were preparing to return to Africa?
derivation: Canonical fact of Book 9: Monica dies at Ostia as the party heads back to Africa. Anchored to Augustine + his mother + the return to Africa; single place answer supported verbatim by 'cum apud Ostia Tiberina essemus, mater defuncta est.' Closed-book, one of the most famous deaths in the Confessions.

author: Augustine
source_text: ut quotquot haec legerint, meminerint ad altare tuum Monnicae, famulae tuae, cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam, quemadmodum nescio.
question: Quo nomine appellatur mater Augustini, quae apud Ostia mortua est?
question_en: By what name is Augustine's mother, who died at Ostia, called?
derivation: Augustine names his mother only here at the close of Book 9. Anchored to Augustine + his mother; single-name answer supported by 'Monnicae, famulae tuae... per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam.' Closed-book (Monica is among the most famous mothers in literature). Spelling 'Monnica' per the text (also Monica).

author: Augustine
source_text: ut quotquot haec legerint, meminerint ad altare tuum Monnicae, famulae tuae, cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam, quemadmodum nescio.
question: Quo nomine appellatur pater Augustini, maritus Monnicae?
question_en: By what name is Augustine's father, the husband of Monnica, called?
derivation: Patricius is named as Monnica's husband and Augustine's parent ('cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me'). Anchored to Augustine + Monnica; single-name answer. Also named at 9.9.19. Closed-book biographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: adiunximus etiam nobis puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter de peccato meo. tu bene feceras eum.
question: Quo nomine appellatur filius quem Augustinus carnaliter genuit?
question_en: By what name is the son whom Augustine begot in the flesh called?
derivation: Augustine's natural son, joined to the group and baptized with him and Alypius at Milan. Anchored to Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter.' Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: adiunximus etiam nobis puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter de peccato meo. tu bene feceras eum. annorum erat ferme quindecim et ingenio praeveniebat multos graves et doctos viros.
question: Quot fere annos natus erat Adeodatus, Augustini filius, eo tempore quo baptizatus est?
question_en: About how many years old was Adeodatus, Augustine's son, at the time he was baptized?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Adeodatus (Augustine's son) at the time of the Milan baptism. Answer mirrors the source's approximative 'ferme' ('annorum erat ferme quindecim'). Short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: est liber noster qui inscribitur 'de magistro': ipse ibi mecum loquitur. tu scis illius esse sensa omnia quae inseruntur ibi ex persona conlocutoris mei, cum esset in annis sedecim.
question: Quo titulo inscribitur liber Augustini in quo filius eius Adeodatus conlocutor inducitur?
question_en: Under what title is the book of Augustine in which his son Adeodatus is brought in as interlocutor inscribed?
derivation: Augustine states that in his dialogue De magistro the interlocutor's words are his son's ('ex persona conlocutoris mei'). Anchored to Augustine + Adeodatus; single title answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (De Magistro is a well-known work).

author: Augustine
source_text: relicto rure Mediolanium remeavimus. placuit et Alypio renasci in te mecum iam induto humilitate sacramentis tuis congrua et fortissimo domitori corporis, usque ad Italicum solum glaciale nudo pede obterendum insolito ausu.
question: Quis amicus Augustini una cum eo Mediolani baptizatus est?
question_en: Which friend of Augustine was baptized at Milan together with him?
derivation: Alypius decided to be 'reborn' (baptized) along with Augustine on their return to Milan ('relicto rure Mediolanium remeavimus. placuit et Alypio renasci in te mecum'). Anchored to Augustine + Milan; single-name answer. Closed-book (Alypius is Augustine's well-known companion).

author: Augustine
source_text: et insinuavi per litteras antistiti tuo, viro sancto Ambrosio, pristinos errores meos et praesens votum meum, ut moneret quid mihi potissimum de libris tuis legendum esset, quo percipiendae tantae gratiae paratior aptiorque fierem. at ille iussit Esaiam prophetam, credo, quod prae ceteris evangelii vocationisque gentium sit praenuntiator apertior.
question: Quem prophetam Augustino legendum antistes Ambrosius iussit?
question_en: Which prophet did the bishop Ambrose order Augustine to read?
derivation: Augustine asked the bishop Ambrose what to read; Ambrose directed him to Isaiah ('at ille iussit Esaiam prophetam'). Anchored to Ambrose (named 'antistiti tuo, viro sancto Ambrosio') + Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quoto anno aetatis suae Monnica, mater Augustini, mortua est?
question_en: In which year of her age did Monnica, Augustine's mother, die?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Monnica: she died in the 56th year of her age ('quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae'). Short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quotum annum aetatis agebat Augustinus cum mater eius Monnica mortua est?
question_en: What year of his age was Augustine in when his mother Monnica died?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Augustine: he was in his 33rd year at his mother's death ('tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae'). Distinct referent from the mother's age; short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quoto die aegritudinis suae Monnica mortua est?
question_en: On which day of her illness did Monnica die?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Monnica: she died on the ninth day of her illness ('die nono aegritudinis suae'). Short, verifiable, closed-book. (Note 9.11.27's 'vix intra quinque dies... decubuit febribus' refers to the acute febrile phase; the explicit death-statement gives the ninth day of the whole illness.)

author: Augustine
source_text: tunc memorato antistiti tuo per visum aperuisti quo loco laterent martyrum corpora Protasii et Gervasii, quae per tot annos incorrupta in thesauro secreti tui reconderas, unde opportune promeres ad cohercendam rabiem femineam sed regiam.
question: Quorum martyrum corpora Ambrosius Mediolani, per visum sibi monstrata, invenit?
question_en: The bodies of which martyrs, revealed to him through a vision, did Ambrose find at Milan?
derivation: The 'antistes' is Ambrose (named in 9.7.15). Through a vision he found the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius ('martyrum corpora Protasii et Gervasii'), later moved to the Ambrosian basilica. Anchored to Ambrose + Milan; two-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (the inventio of SS. Gervasius and Protasius).

author: Augustine
source_text: recordatus sum veridicos versus Ambrosii tui. tu es enim, deus, creator omnium, polique rector vestiens diem decoro lumine, noctem sopora gratia, artus solutos ut quies reddat laboris usui mentesque fessas allevet luctuque solvat anxios.
question: A quo auctore compositi sunt versus 'Deus creator omnium' quos Augustinus post matris suae mortem recordatus est?
question_en: By what author were the verses 'Deus creator omnium,' which Augustine recalled after his mother's death, composed?
derivation: Augustine recalls 'veridicos versus Ambrosii tui' beginning 'deus, creator omnium' — the Ambrosian hymn. Anchored to Augustine + Ambrose; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (a famous Ambrosian hymn). Source_text normalized: per-line quotation marks and a stray bracket stripped, hymn lines joined.

author: Augustine
source_text: fidelis promissor reddis Verecundo pro rure illo eius Cassiciaco, ubi ab aestu saeculi requievimus in te, amoenitatem sempiterne virentis paradisi tui.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur rus Verecundi ubi Augustinus cum suis post conversionem requievit?
question_en: By what name was the country estate of Verecundus, where Augustine and his companions rested after their conversion, called?
derivation: Verecundus's estate where Augustine's party retreated is named Cassiciacum ('pro rure illo eius Cassiciaco, ubi... requievimus'). Anchored to Verecundus + Augustine; single place-name answer (ablative 'Cassiciaco' in text, nom. Cassiciacum). Closed-book (the Cassiciacum retreat/dialogues are famous in Augustine's biography).

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Sub idem tempus Mithridates Pergamenus, magnae nobilitatis domi scientiaeque in bello et virtutis, fidei dignitatisque in amicitia Caesaris, missus in Syriam Ciliciamque initio belli Alexandrini ad auxilia arcessenda, cum magnis copiis, quas celeriter et propensissima civitatium voluntate et sua diligentia confecerat, itinere pedestri, quo coniungitur Aegyptus Syriae, Pelusium adducit
question: Quis initio belli Alexandrini in Syriam Ciliciamque ad auxilia arcessenda missus, magnas copias itinere pedestri in Aegyptum Caesari subsidio adduxit?
question_en: Who, sent to Syria and Cilicia at the start of the Alexandrian war to fetch auxiliaries, led a large army overland into Egypt to relieve Caesar?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Alexandrian war and Caesar's relief: Mithridates of Pergamum gathered forces in Syria and Cilicia and marched overland to Egypt, supported verbatim by 'Mithridates Pergamenus ... missus in Syriam Ciliciamque ... ad auxilia arcessenda, cum magnis copiis ... itinere pedestri ... in Aegyptum'. His relief of the besieged Caesar is closed-book history.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: namque tota Aegyptus maritimo accessu Pharo, pedestri Pelusio velut claustris munita existimatur
question: Quibus duobus claustris, altero ad maritimum accessum, altero ad pedestrem, tota Aegyptus munita esse existimatur?
question_en: By which two strongholds, one guarding the approach by sea, the other by land, is all Egypt thought to be fortified?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Egypt: the Pharos guards the sea approach and Pelusium the land approach, supported verbatim by 'maritimo accessu Pharo, pedestri Pelusio velut claustris munita'. The Pharos of Alexandria and the frontier fortress of Pelusium are closed-book landmarks.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Constat fugisse ex castris regem ipsum receptumque in navem multitudine eorum qui ad proximas navis adnatabant demerso navigio perisse.
question: Quo genere mortis Ptolomaeus rex Aegypti periit, cum victus ex castris ad flumen Nilum fugeret?
question_en: By what kind of death did Ptolemy, king of Egypt, perish when, defeated, he fled from his camp to the river Nile?
answer_en: By the sinking of his boat (he drowned).
derivation: Fact anchored to the boy-king Ptolemy (XIII) and the battle by the Nile: his overloaded boat sank and he drowned, supported verbatim by 'regem ipsum ... demerso navigio perisse'. The king's death in the Nile during the rout is iconic and closed-book; the question supplies the Nile setting established at sections 28-30.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar Aegypto atque Alexandrea potitus reges constituit quos Ptolomaeus testamento scripserat atque obtestatus erat populum Romanum ne mutarentur. Nam maiore ex duobus pueris, rege, amisso minori tradidit regnum maiorique ex duabus filiis, Cleopatrae, quae manserat in fide praesidiisque eius; minorem, Arsinoen, cuius nomine diu regnasse impotenter Ganymeden docuimus, deducere ex regno statuit, ne qua rursus nova dissensio, prius quam diuturnitate confirmarentur regibus imperia, per homines seditiosos nasceretur.
question: Cui Caesar, Aegypto potitus, regnum Aegypti tradidit, quae in fide praesidiisque eius permanserat?
question_en: To whom did Caesar, having taken control of Egypt, hand over the kingdom of Egypt, she who had remained loyal under his protection?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and Egypt: after winning the war he settled the throne on Cleopatra (with the younger surviving brother), supported verbatim by 'maiorique ex duabus filiis, Cleopatrae, quae manserat in fide praesidiisque eius'. Caesar's establishment of Cleopatra on the Egyptian throne is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Nam maiore ex duobus pueris, rege, amisso minori tradidit regnum maiorique ex duabus filiis, Cleopatrae, quae manserat in fide praesidiisque eius; minorem, Arsinoen, cuius nomine diu regnasse impotenter Ganymeden docuimus, deducere ex regno statuit, ne qua rursus nova dissensio, prius quam diuturnitate confirmarentur regibus imperia, per homines seditiosos nasceretur.
question: Quam Ptolomaei filiam minorem Caesar ex regno Aegypti deducere statuit, cuius nomine Ganymedes regnaverat?
question_en: Which younger daughter of Ptolemy did Caesar decide to remove from the kingdom of Egypt, in whose name Ganymedes had reigned?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and the Egyptian settlement: he removed the younger sister Arsinoe (IV), in whose name the eunuch Ganymedes had ruled, supported verbatim by 'minorem, Arsinoen ... deducere ex regno statuit'. Arsinoe, later led in Caesar's triumph, is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Interfecta multitudine omni suorum aut capta Pharnaces cum paucis equitibus profugit; cui nisi castrorum oppugnatio facultatem attulisset liberius profugiendi, vivus in Caesaris potestatem adductus esset.
question: Quem regem Caesar apud Zelam in Ponto acie fudit, ita ut is cum paucis equitibus profugeret?
question_en: Which king did Caesar rout in battle at Zela in Pontus, so that he fled with a few horsemen?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and the battle of Zela (Zela located in Pontus at section 72): Pharnaces was crushed and fled with few horsemen, supported verbatim by 'Pharnaces cum paucis equitibus profugit'. Caesar's lightning victory over Pharnaces at Zela (the 'veni vidi vici' battle) is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Quo tamen incommodo Domitius accepto reliquias exercitus dissipati collegit itineribusque tutis per Cappadociam se in Asiam recepit.
question: Quis Romanus imperator, apud Nicopolim a Pharnace superatus, cum reliquiis exercitus per Cappadociam in Asiam se recepit?
question_en: Which Roman commander, defeated by Pharnaces at Nicopolis, withdrew with the remnants of his army through Cappadocia into Asia?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Pharnaces and Nicopolis (the town in Armenia minor, section 36): Domitius Calvinus, beaten in the battle that preceded Zela, gathered his shattered army and retreated through Cappadocia into Asia, supported verbatim by 'Domitius ... reliquias exercitus dissipati collegit itineribusque ... per Cappadociam se in Asiam recepit'. Pharnaces' defeat of Domitius Calvinus is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Dum haec in Aegypto geruntur, rex Deiotarus ad Domitium Calvinum, cui Caesar Asiam finitimasque provincias administrandas tradiderat, venit oratum ne Armeniam minorem, regnum suum, neve Cappadociam, regnum Ariobarzanis, possideri vastarique pateretur a Pharnace; quo malo nisi liberarentur, imperata se facere pecuniamque promissam Caesari non posse persolvere.
question: Cuius regis regnum erat Cappadocia, quam Deiotarus a Pharnace defendi orabat?
question_en: Of which king was Cappadocia the kingdom, which Deiotarus begged be defended from Pharnaces?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Cappadocia and the appeal against Pharnaces: Cappadocia is the kingdom of Ariobarzanes, supported verbatim by 'Cappadociam, regnum Ariobarzanis'. Ariobarzanes (III) of Cappadocia is closed-book; the question pins it with Deiotarus and Pharnaces.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Deiotarus, tetrarches Gallograeciae tum quidem paene totius, quod ei neque legibus neque moribus concessum esse ceteri tetrarchae contendebant, sine dubio autem rex Armeniae minoris ab senatu appellatus, depositis regiis insignibus neque tantum privato vestitu sed etiam reorum habitu supplex ad Caesarem venit oratum ut sibi ignosceret
question: Quo regio titulo Deiotarus, Gallograeciae tetrarches, ab senatu Romano appellatus erat?
question_en: By what royal title had Deiotarus, tetrarch of Galatia, been named by the Roman senate?
derivation: Title fact anchored to Deiotarus, tetrarch of Galatia: the senate had named him king of Armenia minor, supported verbatim by 'rex Armeniae minoris ab senatu appellatus'. Deiotarus (Cicero's client-king) is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Mithridaten Pergamenum, a quo rem feliciter celeriterque gestam in Aegypto supra scripsimus, regio genere ortum, disciplinis etiam regiis educatum — nam eum Mithridates, rex Asiae totius, propter nobilitatem Pergamo parvulum secum asportaverat in castra multosque retinuerat annos — regem Bosphori constituit, quod sub imperio Pharnacis fuerat, provinciasque populi Romani a barbaris atque inimicis regibus interposito amicissimo rege munivit.
question: Cuius regni regem Caesar Mithridaten Pergamenum constituit, quod antea sub imperio Pharnacis fuerat?
question_en: Of which kingdom did Caesar make Mithridates of Pergamum king, a realm that had previously been under Pharnaces' rule?
derivation: Office fact anchored to Caesar, Mithridates of Pergamum, and Pharnaces: as a reward Caesar made Mithridates king of the Bosphorus, the realm formerly Pharnaces', supported verbatim by 'regem Bosphori constituit, quod sub imperio Pharnacis fuerat'. Closed-book reward of the man who relieved Caesar in Egypt.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sic vocibus consulis, terrore praesentis exercitus, minis amicorum Pompei plerique compulsi inviti et coacti Scipionis sententiam sequuntur: uti ante certam diem Caesar exercitum dimittat; si non faciat, eum adversus rem publicam facturum videri. Intercedit M. Antonius, Q. Cassius, tribuni plebis.
question: Qui duo tribuni plebis sententiae, ut Caesar exercitum dimitteret, intercesserunt?
question_en: Which two tribunes of the plebs vetoed the motion that Caesar should disband his army?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the senate's decree that Caesar disband his army; the two named tribunes (Mark Antony and Q. Cassius Longinus) who interposed the veto are given verbatim ('Intercedit M. Antonius, Q. Cassius, tribuni plebis'). The veto and the tribunes' subsequent flight to Caesar are the iconic opening of the civil war; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Profugiunt statim ex urbe tribuni plebis seseque ad Caesarem conferunt. Is eo tempore erat Ravennae exspectabatque suis lenissimis postulatis responsa.
question: In quo oppido erat Caesar, cum tribuni plebis ex urbe profugientes ad eum se contulerunt?
question_en: In what town was Caesar when the tribunes of the plebs fled the city and came to him?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar and the fleeing tribunes; locative answer supported verbatim by 'Is eo tempore erat Ravennae'. Caesar's position at Ravenna at the outbreak of the war is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Conclamant legionis XIII, quae aderat, milites—hanc enim initio tumultus evocaverat, reliquae nondum convenerant—sese paratos esse imperatoris sui tribunorumque plebis iniurias defendere.
question: Cuius legionis milites, quae sola initio tumultus aderat, se paratos esse Caesaris tribunorumque plebis iniurias defendere conclamaverunt?
question_en: The soldiers of which legion, the only one present at the start of the disturbance, shouted that they were ready to defend the wrongs done to Caesar and the tribunes of the plebs?
derivation: Number/name fact anchored to Caesar and the start of the war; answer (legio XIII) supported verbatim, including 'quae aderat' and 'reliquae nondum convenerant' (only the Thirteenth was present). The legion that crossed the Rubicon with Caesar; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Cognita militum voluntate Ariminum cum ea legione proficiscitur ibique tribunos plebis, qui ad eum profugerant, convenit.
question: In quod oppidum Caesar cum legione XIII primum profectus est, ubi tribunos plebis profugos convenit?
question_en: To which town did Caesar first advance with the Thirteenth Legion, where he met the fugitive tribunes of the plebs?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar and the Thirteenth Legion; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Ariminum cum ea legione proficiscitur ibique tribunos plebis ... convenit'. Caesar's first seizure across the Rubicon; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Cum his ad Domitium Ahenobarbum Corfinium magnis itineribus pervenit Caesaremque adesse cum legionibus duabus nuntiat.
question: Ad quem Pompeianorum ducem Caesar Corfinium magnis itineribus pervenit?
question_en: Against which Pompeian commander did Caesar march to Corfinium by forced marches?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Corfinium and Caesar; single named answer supported verbatim by 'ad Domitium Ahenobarbum Corfinium ... pervenit' (the praenomen L. given at 1.23). Domitius Ahenobarbus, besieged at Corfinium and there pardoned by Caesar, is closed-book history.

author: Caesar
source_text: Pompeius his rebus cognitis, quae erant ad Corfinium gestae, Luceria proficiscitur Canusium atque inde Brundisium.
question: In quod oppidum maritimum Pompeius, cognitis rebus ad Corfinium gestis, Luceria per Canusium se recepit?
question_en: To which coastal town did Pompey withdraw, by way of Luceria and Canusium, once he learned of the events at Corfinium?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Pompey and Corfinium; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Luceria proficiscitur Canusium atque inde Brundisium'. Pompey's retreat to Brundisium is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Reperit consules Dyrrachium profectos cum magna parte exercitus, Pompeium remanere Brundisii cum cohortibus viginti.
question: Quo profectos esse consules Caesar, Brundisium cum legionibus perveniens, repperit?
question_en: Where had the consuls departed to, as Caesar found when he arrived at Brundisium with his legions?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the consuls, Brundisium, and Caesar; single answer supported verbatim by 'consules Dyrrachium profectos'. The consuls' crossing of the Adriatic to Greece is closed-book. Acc.+inf. 'profectos esse' under repperit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Mittit in Sardiniam cum legione una Valerium legatum, in Siciliam Curionem pro praetore cum legionibus duabus; eundem, cum Siciliam recepisset, protinus in Africam traducere exercitum iubet. Sardiniam obtinebat M. Cotta, Siciliam M. Cato; Africam sorte Tubero obtinere debebat.
question: Quis ex Pompeianis Siciliam obtinebat, quam Caesar Curionem occupare iussit?
question_en: Who held Sicily for the Pompeians, the province Caesar ordered Curio to seize?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Sicily and Curio; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Siciliam M. Cato [obtinebat]', with Curio sent there with two legions. Cato Uticensis abandoning Sicily before Curio is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Quibus effectis armatisque diebus XXX, a qua die materia caesa est, adductisque Massiliam his D. Brutum praeficit, C. Trebonium legatum ad oppugnationem Massiliae relinquit.
question: Quem legatum Caesar ad oppugnationem Massiliae reliquit?
question_en: Which legate did Caesar leave in charge of the siege of Massilia?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Massilia and Caesar; single named answer supported verbatim by 'C. Trebonium legatum ad oppugnationem Massiliae relinquit' (D. Brutus being set over the fleet). The siege of Massilia under Trebonius is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Afranius et Petreius et Varro, legati Pompei, quorum unus Hispaniam citeriorem tribus legionibus, alter ulteriorem a saltu Castulonensi ad Anam duabus legionibus, tertius ab Ana Vettonum agrum Lusitaniamque pari numero legionum optinebat.
question: Qui tres legati Pompei initio belli civilis Hispanias obtinebant?
question_en: Which three legates of Pompey held the Spanish provinces at the outbreak of the civil war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Pompey and the Spanish provinces; the three named legates are given verbatim ('Afranius et Petreius et Varro, legati Pompei'). Pompey's Spanish command is closed-book; answer is the closed set of three.

author: Caesar
source_text: Quibus coactis celeriter Petreius per Vettones ad Afranium pervenit, constituuntque communi consilio bellum ad Ilerdam propter ipsius opportunitatem gerere.
question: Ad quod oppidum Afranius et Petreius communi consilio bellum gerere constituerunt?
question_en: At which town did Afranius and Petreius jointly decide to wage the war?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Afranius and Petreius; single named answer supported verbatim by 'bellum ad Ilerdam ... gerere'. The campaign of Ilerda is the central episode of Book I; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Caesar legiones in Hispaniam praemiserat VI, auxilia peditum V milia, equitum III milia.
question: Quot legiones Caesar in Hispaniam praemisit?
question_en: How many legions did Caesar send ahead into Spain?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar and Spain; answer (VI = six) supported verbatim by 'legiones in Hispaniam praemiserat VI' and echoed at 1.85 ('sex legiones ... missas in Hispaniam'). Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Fabius finitimarum civitatum animos litteris nuntiisque temptabat. In Sicori flumine pontes effecerat duos distantes inter se milia passuum IIII.
question: In quo flumine apud Ilerdam C. Fabius, Caesaris legatus, duos pontes effecit?
question_en: In which river near Ilerda did Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius build two bridges?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Fabius and Ilerda; single named answer supported verbatim by 'In Sicori flumine pontes effecerat duos'. The Sicoris (Segre) is the river of the Ilerda campaign; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Petreius atque Afranius cum stipendium ab legionibus paene seditione facta flagitarentur, cuius illi diem nondum venisse dicerent, Caesar ut cognosceret, postulatum est, eoque utrique, quod statuit, contenti fuerunt. Parte circiter tertia exercitus eo biduo dimissa duas legiones suas antecedere, reliquas subsequi iussit, ut non longo inter se spatio castra facerent, eique negotio Q. Fufium Calenum legatum praeficit. Hoc eius praescripto ex Hispania ad Varum flumen est iter factum, atque ibi reliqua pars exercitus dimissa est.
question: Ad quod flumen exercitus Afranii et Petreii in Hispania victus a Caesare dimissus est?
question_en: To which river was the defeated army of Afranius and Petreius led from Spain and disbanded?
derivation: Place/outcome fact anchored to Afranius and Petreius (named in the same paragraph) and Spain; single named answer supported verbatim by 'ex Hispania ad Varum flumen est iter factum, atque ibi reliqua pars exercitus dimissa est'. The surrender and disbandment of the Pompeian army in Spain is the climax of Book I; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Massilia enim fere tribus ex oppidi partibus mari alluitur; reliqua quarta est, quae aditum habeat ab terra.
question: Quot fere ex partibus Massilia mari alluitur, ut Caesar scribit?
question_en: On about how many sides is Massilia washed by the sea, as Caesar writes?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Massilia + Caesar; number answer supported verbatim by 'fere tribus ex oppidi partibus mari alluitur', with only the fourth (landward) side accessible by foot. 'fere' mirrors the source's approximation. Massilia as a sea-girt city under siege is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Conspicataeque naves triremes duae navem D. Bruti, quae ex insigni facile agnosci poterat, duabus ex partibus sese in eam incitaverant. Sed tantum re provisa Brutus celeritate navis enisus est, ut parvo momento antecederet. Illae adeo graviter inter se incitatae conflixerunt, ut vehementissime utraque ex concursu laborarent, altera vero praefracto rostro tota collabefieret. Qua re animadversa, quae proximae ei loco ex Bruti classe naves erant, in eas impeditas impetum faciunt celeriterque ambas deprimunt.
question: Quis classi Caesaris in proeliis navalibus apud Massiliam praefuit?
question_en: Who commanded Caesar's fleet in the naval battles at Massilia?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar + Massilia; D. Brutus's flagship (marked by its 'insigne') and the phrase 'ex Bruti classe naves' show he commanded Caesar's fleet in the sea fighting. Complements DBC 1.36, where Caesar set D. Brutus over the fleet and Trebonius over the land siege; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Massilienses arma tormentaque ex oppido, ut est imperatum, proferunt, naves ex portu navalibusque educunt, pecuniam ex publico tradunt. Quibus rebus confectis Caesar magis eos pro nomine et vetustate, quam pro meritis in se civitatis conservans duas ibi legiones praesidio relinquit, ceteras in Italiam mittit; ipse ad urbem proficiscitur.
question: Quot legiones Caesar in oppido Massilia, postquam in deditionem venit, praesidio reliquit?
question_en: How many legions did Caesar leave as a garrison in the town of Massilia after it surrendered?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar + Massilia; answer supported verbatim by 'duas ibi legiones praesidio relinquit'. The surrender (handing over arms, ships, and money) is in the source; the fall of Massilia is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Eadem ratione privatim ac publice quibusdam civitatibus habitis honoribus Tarracone discedit pedibusque Narbonem atque inde Massiliam pervenit. Ibi legem de dictatore latam seseque dictatorem dictum a M. Lepido praetore cognoscit.
question: A quo praetore Caesar, cum Massiliam pervenisset, se dictatorem dictum esse cognovit?
question_en: By which praetor did Caesar, when he reached Massilia, learn that he had been named dictator?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar + Massilia; acc.+inf. 'se dictatorem dictum esse' under cognovit, with the agent supported verbatim by 'dictatorem dictum a M. Lepido praetore'. M. Aemilius Lepidus' law naming Caesar dictator in 49 BC is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: M. Varro in ulteriore Hispania initio cognitis eis rebus, quae sunt in Italia gestae, diffidens Pompeianis rebus amicissime de Caesare loquebatur: praecoccupatum sese legatione ab Cn. Pompeio teneri obstrictum fide.
question: Quis Pompei legatus initio belli civilis ulteriorem Hispaniam obtinebat?
question_en: Which legate of Pompey held Further Spain at the start of the civil war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Pompey + Further Spain; supported by 'M. Varro in ulteriore Hispania ... legatione ab Cn. Pompeio teneri obstrictum fide'. M. Terentius Varro, Pompey's legate in Further Spain who later surrendered to Caesar; closed-book. Distinct from P. Attius Varus in Africa.

author: Caesar
source_text: Eisdem temporibus C. Curio in Africam profectus ex Sicilia et iam ab initio copias P. Attii Vari despiciens duas legiones ex IIII, quas a Caesare acceperat, D equites transportabat.
question: Cuius ducis Pompeiani copias C. Curio, in Africam ex Sicilia transgressus, ab initio despexit?
question_en: Whose Pompeian forces did Curio, having crossed from Sicily into Africa, despise from the start?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Curio + Africa; P. Attius Varus, the Pompeian commander in Africa, named verbatim ('copias P. Attii Vari despiciens'), with the source's own verb (despiciens) echoed. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Eodemque tempore his rebus subsidio DC Numidae ex oppido peditesque CCCC mittuntur a Varo, quos auxilii causa rex Iuba paucis diebus ante Uticam miserat.
question: Quis rex Numidarum P. Attio Varo apud Uticam auxilia adversus Curionem misit?
question_en: Which king of the Numidians sent auxiliaries to Publius Attius Varus at Utica against Curio?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Varus + Utica + Curio; supported verbatim by 'rex Iuba ... Uticam miserat', the Numidian troops then deployed by Varus ('mittuntur a Varo'). Juba's intervention on the Pompeian side in Africa is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Huic et paternum hospitium cum Pompeio et simultas cum Curione intercedebat, quod tribunus plebis legem promulgaverat, qua lege regnum Iubae publicaverat.
question: Cuius regis regnum C. Curio, cum tribunus plebis esset, lege promulgata publicare conatus erat?
question_en: Whose kingdom had Curio, when he was tribune of the plebs, sought to confiscate by a promulgated law?
derivation: Legal/name fact anchored to Curio (as tribune) + Juba; supported verbatim by 'tribunus plebis legem promulgaverat, qua lege regnum Iubae publicaverat'. The tribune is Curio (50 BC), and this law is given as the cause of Juba's enmity ('simultas cum Curione'); closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Curio Marcium Uticam navibus praemittit; ipse eodem cum exercitu proficiscitur biduique iter progressus ad flumen Bagradam pervenit.
question: Ad quod flumen in Africa C. Curio cum exercitu pervenit?
question_en: To which river in Africa did Curio arrive with his army?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Curio + Africa; answer supported verbatim by 'ad flumen Bagradam pervenit'. The Bagradas, river of Curio's fatal African campaign (Saburra's camp lay on it, 2.38-39), is the recognizable name of his defeat; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Iuba certior factus a Saburra de nocturno proelio II milia Hispanorum et Gallorum equitum, quos suae custodiae causa circum se habere consuerat, et peditum eam partem, cui maxime confidebat, Saburrae submisit; ipse cum reliquis copiis elephantisque LX lentius subsequitur.
question: Cuius regis copiis subsidio missis fretus Saburra exercitum C. Curionis in Africa delevit?
question_en: Backed by which king's reinforcements did Saburra destroy Curio's army in Africa?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Saburra + Curio. Saburra, called Juba's praefectus at 2.38 ('Saburram, eius praefectum'), routed Curio with cavalry and picked infantry that King Juba sent up ('Saburrae submisit'), Juba himself following with 60 elephants; the army's destruction follows at 2.41-42. Juba is the Numidian king who defeated Curio; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: At Curio numquam se amisso exercitu, quem a Caesare fidei commissum acceperit, in eius conspectum reversurum confirmat atque ita proelians interficitur.
question: Quis Caesaris dux in Africa, amisso exercitu, ad Caesarem reverti recusans proelians interfectus est?
question_en: Which of Caesar's commanders in Africa, having lost his army, refused to return to Caesar and was killed fighting?
derivation: Name/outcome fact anchored to Caesar + Africa; supported verbatim by 'Curio ... in eius conspectum reversurum confirmat atque ita proelians interficitur'. His army was destroyed to the last man ('Milites ad unum omnes interficiuntur', same chapter). Curio's death with his army at the Bagradas is among the most famous episodes of the African campaign; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Dictatore habente comitia Caesare consules creantur Iulius Caesar et P. Servilius: is enim erat annus, quo per leges ei consulem fieri liceret.
question: Quis fuit collega Caesaris in consulatu eo anno, quo Pompeium acie in Thessalia superavit?
question_en: Who was Caesar's colleague in the consulship in the year in which he defeated Pompey in battle in Thessaly?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and his consulship of 48 BC (the year of Pharsalus); single named answer supported verbatim by 'consules creantur Iulius Caesar et P. Servilius'. Caesar's colleague P. Servilius Isauricus is closed-book history; the Thessaly anchor fixes the year.

author: Caesar
source_text: Eo legiones XII, equitatum omnem venire iusserat. Sed tantum navium repperit, ut anguste XV milia legionariorum militum, DC equites transportari possent.
question: Quot fere legionarios milites et quot equites Caesar primo transitu ex Brundisio in Graeciam transportare potuit?
answer: Quindecim milia militum et sescentos equites.
question_en: About how many legionary soldiers and how many cavalry could Caesar transport in his first crossing from Brundisium to Greece?
answer_en: Fifteen thousand soldiers and six hundred cavalry.
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar and the crossing of the Adriatic from Brundisium; the figures (XV milia, DC) are supported verbatim by 'XV milia legionariorum militum, DC equites transportari possent'. Caesar's shortage of ships for the bold winter crossing is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Praeerat Aegyptiis navibus Pompeius filius, Asiaticis D. Laelius et C. Triarius, Syriacis C. Cassius, Rhodiis C. Marcellus cum C. Coponio, Liburnicae atque Achaicae classi Scribonius Libo et M. Octavius. Toti tamen officio maritimo M. Bibulus praepositus cuncta administrabat; ad hunc summa imperii respiciebat.
question: Quis toti officio maritimo Pompeianae partis praepositus erat, penes quem summa imperii navalis erat?
question_en: Who was placed in charge of all naval affairs on Pompey's side, with whom rested the supreme command of the fleet?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Pompey's fleet; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Toti tamen officio maritimo M. Bibulus praepositus cuncta administrabat; ad hunc summa imperii respiciebat'. M. Bibulus, Caesar's old consular colleague, as Pompey's fleet commander is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sed cum prope Dyrrachium Pompeius constitisset castraque metari iussisset, perterrito etiam tum exercitu princeps Labienus procedit iuratque se eum non deserturum eundemque casum subiturum, quemcumque ei fortuna tribuisset.
question: Apud utrum imperatorem, Caesarem an Pompeium, T. Labienus bello civili stetit?
question_en: On which commander's side, Caesar's or Pompey's, did Titus Labienus stand in the civil war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to T. Labienus, Caesar's chief legate in Gaul; that he had gone over to Pompey is supported by his swearing never to desert him ('se eum non deserturum'). Labienus' defection to Pompey is iconic and closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Erant enim circum castra Pompei permulti editi atque asperi colles. Hos primum praesidiis tenuit castellaque ibi communit. Inde, ut loci cuiusque natura ferebat, ex castello in castellum perducta munitione circumvallare Pompeium instituit.
question: Quem ducem Caesar apud Dyrrachium continuatis munitionibus circumvallare instituit?
question_en: Which commander did Caesar undertake to encircle with continuous fortifications at Dyrrachium?
derivation: Operation fact anchored to Caesar and Dyrrachium; single named answer supported verbatim by 'circumvallare Pompeium instituit'. The lines of Dyrrachium, where Caesar blockaded Pompey, are closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Pompeius eo proelio imperator est appellatus. Hoc nomen obtinuit atque ita se postea salutari passus est, sed neque in litteris scribere est solitus, neque in fascibus insignia laureae praetulit.
question: Quo nomine Pompeius post proelium ad Dyrrachium, ubi Caesarem reppulit, ab exercitu suo appellatus est?
question_en: By what name was Pompey hailed by his army after the battle at Dyrrachium, where he repulsed Caesar?
derivation: Title fact anchored to Pompey and the battle at Dyrrachium; supported verbatim by 'Pompeius eo proelio imperator est appellatus' (eo proelio = the Dyrrachium engagement). Caesar's repulse at Dyrrachium and Pompey's acclamation as imperator are closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Pompeius, iam cum intra vallum nostri versarentur, equum nactus, detractis insignibus imperatoris, decumana porta se ex castris eiecit protinusque equo citato Larisam contendit.
question: In quod Thessaliae oppidum Pompeius statim ex castris victus profugit, postquam acie a Caesare superatus est?
question_en: To which town of Thessaly did the defeated Pompey flee straight from his camp after he was beaten in battle by Caesar?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Pompey and his defeat by Caesar (Pharsalus, in Thessaly); single named answer supported verbatim by 'equo citato Larisam contendit'. Pompey's immediate flight to Larisa after Pharsalus is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: In eo proelio non amplius CC milites desideravit, sed centuriones, fortes viros, circiter XXX amisit.
question: Quot fere milites Caesar in proelio, quo Pompeium in Thessalia devicit, amisisse se scribit?
question_en: About how many soldiers does Caesar say he lost in the battle in which he decisively defeated Pompey in Thessaly?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar and the battle that defeated Pompey (Pharsalus); supported verbatim by 'non amplius CC milites desideravit'. The famously light Caesarian losses at Pharsalus are closed-book; eo proelio = the Pharsalus battle, supplied by the question.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ex Pompeiano exercitu circiter milia XV cecidisse videbantur, sed in deditionem venerunt amplius milia XXIIII.
question: Quot fere milia hominum ex Pompei exercitu in proelio Thessalico cecidisse Caesar tradit?
question_en: About how many thousands of men from Pompey's army does Caesar report fell in the Thessalian (Pharsalus) battle?
derivation: Number fact self-anchored to Pompey's army; supported verbatim by 'Ex Pompeiano exercitu circiter milia XV cecidisse videbantur'. The lopsided casualties at Pharsalus (against Caesar's ~200) are closed-book; indirect statement 'cecidisse ... tradit'.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ibi casu rex erat Ptolomaeus, puer aetate, magnis copiis cum sorore Cleopatra bellum gerens, quam paucis ante mensibus per suos propinquos atque amicos regno expulerat.
question: Quis Aegypti rex erat, cum Pompeius profugus eo pervenit?
question_en: Who was king of Egypt when the fugitive Pompey arrived there?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Egypt and Pompey's arrival; supported verbatim by 'rex erat Ptolomaeus, puer aetate'. The boy-king Ptolemy (XIII) at the time of Pompey's death is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ibi casu rex erat Ptolomaeus, puer aetate, magnis copiis cum sorore Cleopatra bellum gerens, quam paucis ante mensibus per suos propinquos atque amicos regno expulerat.
question: Cum qua sorore, quam regno expulerat, Ptolomaeus rex Aegypti eo tempore bellum gerebat?
question_en: With which sister, whom he had driven from the kingdom, was Ptolemy, king of Egypt, then at war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Ptolemy, king of Egypt; supported verbatim by 'cum sorore Cleopatra bellum gerens, quam ... regno expulerat'. The war between Ptolemy and his sister Cleopatra is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ipsi clam consilio inito Achillam, praefectum regium, singulari hominem audacia, et L. Septimium, tribunum militum, ad interficiendum Pompeium miserunt. Ab his liberaliter ipse appellatus et quadam notitia Septimii productus, quod bello praedonum apud eum ordinem duxerat, naviculam parvulam conscendit cum paucis suis: ibi ab Achilla et Septimio interficitur.
question: A quibus duobus viris Pompeius in Aegyptum profugus interfectus est?
question_en: By which two men was Pompey killed when he had fled to Egypt?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Pompey and Egypt; the two killers are supported verbatim ('Achillam, praefectum regium ... et L. Septimium, tribunum militum, ad interficiendum Pompeium miserunt ... ab Achilla et Septimio interficitur'). Pompey's murder on arrival in Egypt is iconic and closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Alexandriae de Pompei morte cognoscit atque ibi primum e nave egrediens clamorem militum audit, quos rex in oppido praesidii causa reliquerat.
question: In quo Aegypti oppido Caesar, Pompeium persecutus, de eius morte cognovit?
question_en: In which Egyptian city did Caesar, having pursued Pompey, learn of his death?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar and Pompey; single answer supported verbatim by 'Alexandriae de Pompei morte cognoscit'. Caesar's arrival at Alexandria, where he learned of Pompey's murder, is closed-book and opens the Alexandrian war.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Tum Considius, 'Unus est' inquit 'Scipio imperator hoc tempore populi Romani'.
question: Quem Considius unum eo tempore imperatorem populi Romani esse adfirmavit?
question_en: Whom did Considius declare to be the one commander (imperator) of the Roman people at that time?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Considius (the Pompeian commander of Hadrumetum) and Scipio. Refusing Caesar's title, Considius names Q. Caecilius Metellus Scipio as the sole imperator, supported verbatim by 'Unus est Scipio imperator hoc tempore populi Romani'. That Scipio was the supreme commander of the Republican forces in Africa is closed-book history.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Hostes interim quorum dux erat Labienus et duo Pacidei, aciem derigunt mirabili longitudine non peditum, sed equitum confertam.
question: Quis cum duobus Pacideis adversariorum aciem equitum confertam contra Caesarem in Africa direxit?
question_en: Who, together with the two Pacidei, drew up the enemy's dense battle line of cavalry against Caesar in Africa?
derivation: Name fact anchored to T. Labienus and the Pacidei; supported verbatim by 'quorum dux erat Labienus et duo Pacidei, aciem derigunt ... equitum confertam'. Labienus, Caesar's former Gallic legate, commanding the Republican cavalry in the African war is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Cum praesertim ab incolis eius provinciae nuntiarentur adversariorum copiae: equitatus infinitus, legiones regiae IIII, levis armaturae magna vis, Scipionis legiones X, elephanti CXX classesque esse complures.
question: Quot elephantos adversarii Caesaris in Africa habere nuntiabantur?
question_en: How many elephants were Caesar's adversaries reported to have in Africa?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the Republican and royal forces in Africa; supported verbatim by 'elephanti CXX'. The reported enemy array Caesar faced (ten Scipionian legions, 120 elephants) is framed by the text's own 'nuntiarentur'; the war-elephants of the African war are closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar trinis castris potitus occisisque hostium X milibus fugatisque compluribus se recepit L militibus amissis, paucis sauciis in castra, ac statim ex itinere ante oppidum Thapsum constitit elephantosque LXIIII ornatos armatosque cum turribus ornamentisque capit.
question: Ad quod oppidum maritimum Caesar Scipionis Iubaeque copias acie devicit?
question_en: At which coastal town did Caesar defeat in battle the forces of Scipio and Juba?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar against Scipio and Juba. The rout (three camps taken, 10,000 slain) and Caesar's halt 'ante oppidum Thapsum' are supported verbatim; the battle of Thapsus (46 BC) that destroyed the Republican army is among the best-known facts of the civil wars.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar trinis castris potitus occisisque hostium X milibus fugatisque compluribus se recepit L militibus amissis, paucis sauciis in castra, ac statim ex itinere ante oppidum Thapsum constitit elephantosque LXIIII ornatos armatosque cum turribus ornamentisque capit.
question: Quot elephantos Caesar post pugnam ad Thapsum captos cepit?
question_en: How many elephants did Caesar capture after the battle at Thapsus?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar and Thapsus; supported verbatim by 'elephantosque LXIIII ... capit'. The sixty-four war-elephants taken after Thapsus are closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar trinis castris potitus occisisque hostium X milibus fugatisque compluribus se recepit L militibus amissis, paucis sauciis in castra, ac statim ex itinere ante oppidum Thapsum constitit elephantosque LXIIII ornatos armatosque cum turribus ornamentisque capit.
question: Quot fere hostium milia ad Thapsum occisa sunt et quot milites Caesar in ea victoria amisit?
question_en: About how many thousands of the enemy were killed at Thapsus, and how many soldiers did Caesar lose in that victory?
answer_en: Ten thousand of the enemy; fifty of his own.
derivation: Number fact anchored to Caesar and Thapsus; supported verbatim by 'occisis hostium X milibus ... L militibus amissis'. The lopsided casualties of Thapsus (about 10,000 enemy dead against about 50 Caesarians) are closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: C. Interim Vergilius postquam terra marique clausus se nihil proficere intellexit suosque interfectos aut fugatos, M. Catonem Uticae sibi ipsum manus attulisse, regem vagum ab suisque desertum ab omnibus aspernari, Saburram eiusque copias ab Sittio esse deletas, Uticae Caesarem sine mora receptum, de tanto exercitu reliquias esse nullas, ipse sibi suisque liberis a C. Caninio proconsule qui eum obsidebat, fide accepta seque et sua omnia et oppidum proconsuli tradit.
question: In quo oppido Africae M. Cato sibi ipse mortem conscivit?
question_en: In which town of Africa did Marcus Cato take his own life?
derivation: Place and name fact anchored to M. Cato; supported verbatim by 'M. Catonem Uticae sibi ipsum manus attulisse'. Cato's suicide at Utica after the Thapsus disaster, the source of his cognomen Uticensis, is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Rex interim ab omnibus civitatibus exclusus desperata salute, cum iam cenatus esset, cum Petreio, ut cum virtute interfecti esse viderentur, ferro inter se depugnant, atque firmior imbecilliorem Iubam Petreius facile ferro consumpsit.
question: A quo rex Iuba, postquam ab omnibus civitatibus exclusus est, ferro depugnans interfectus est?
question_en: By whom was King Juba, after he had been shut out by all the towns, killed fighting with the sword?
derivation: Name fact anchored to King Juba and M. Petreius; supported verbatim by 'imbecilliorem Iubam Petreius facile ferro consumpsit'. The death-pact duel in which Petreius killed the fugitive Juba of Numidia is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Scipio interim cum Damasippo et Torquato et Plaetorio Rustiano navibus longis diu multumque iactati cum Hispaniam peterent, ad Hipponem Regium deferuntur, ubi classis P. Sitti ad id tempus erat. A qua pauciora ab amplioribus circumventa navigia deprimuntur, ibique Scipio cum quos paulo ante nominavi interiit.
question: Apud quod oppidum Scipio, classe P. Sittii circumventus, in mari periit?
question_en: Off which town did Scipio, surrounded by the fleet of Publius Sittius, perish at sea?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Scipio and Sittius's fleet; supported verbatim by 'ad Hipponem Regium deferuntur ... ibique Scipio ... interiit'. Scipio's death at sea off Hippo Regius while fleeing toward Spain after Thapsus is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Itaque omnibus insciis neque suspicantibus vigilia tertia iubet omnes legiones extra castra educi atque se consequi ad oppidum Ruspinam versus, in quo ipse praesidium habuit et quod primum ad amicitiam eius accessit.
question: Quod oppidum Africae primum ad Caesaris amicitiam accessit?
question_en: Which town of Africa was the first to come over to Caesar's friendship?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar and Ruspina; supported verbatim by 'ad oppidum Ruspinam ... quod primum ad amicitiam eius accessit'. Ruspina, Caesar's base of operations and the first African town to side with him, is closed-book for this campaign.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Rex interim Iuba ut ex proelio fugerat, una cum Petreio interdiu in villis latitando tandem nocturnis itineribus confectis in regnum pervenit atque ad oppidum Zamam, ubi ipse domicilium coniuges liberosque habebat, quo ex cuncto regno omnem pecuniam carissimasque res comportaverat quodque inito bello operibus maximis muniverat, accedit.
question: In quo oppido regni sui rex Iuba domicilium coniugesque et liberos habebat?
question_en: In which town of his kingdom did King Juba have his residence, his wives, and his children?
derivation: Place fact anchored to King Juba; supported verbatim by 'ad oppidum Zamam, ubi ipse domicilium coniuges liberosque habebat'. Zama as Juba's royal seat, which barred its returning king after Thapsus, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen, a Belgis Matrona et Sequana dividit.
question: Quod flumen, ut Caesar scribit, Gallos ab Aquitanis dividit?
question_en: Which river, as Caesar writes, divides the Gauls from the Aquitani?
derivation: Geography fact of the famous opening chapter. Anchored to the Gauls, the Aquitani, and Caesar; single river answer supported verbatim by 'Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen ... dividit'. Closed-book staple of Latin geography.

author: Caesar
source_text: Apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus fuit et ditissimus Orgetorix.
question: Quis apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus ac ditissimus fuit?
question_en: Who was by far the noblest and richest man among the Helvetii?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Helvetii; single named answer supported verbatim. Orgetorix is the well-known instigator of the Helvetian migration; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Pro multitudine autem hominum et pro gloria belli atque fortitudinis angustos se fines habere arbitrabantur, qui in longitudinem milia passuum CCXL, in latitudinem CLXXX patebant.
question: Quot milia passuum in longitudinem fines Helvetiorum patebant?
question_en: How many miles in length did the territory of the Helvetii extend?
derivation: Measure fact anchored to the Helvetii; number answer (CCXL = 240) supported verbatim, the width being CLXXX. The guidelines list exactly this kind of distance fact as a target.

author: Caesar
source_text: Id hoc facilius iis persuasit, quod undique loci natura Helvetii continentur: una ex parte flumine Rheno latissimo atque altissimo, qui agrum Helvetium a Germanis dividit; altera ex parte monte Iura altissimo, qui est inter Sequanos et Helvetios; tertia lacu Lemanno et flumine Rhodano, qui provinciam nostram ab Helvetiis dividit.
question: Qui mons inter Sequanos et Helvetios situs est?
question_en: Which mountain lies between the Sequani and the Helvetii?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to the Sequani and Helvetii; single answer supported verbatim by 'monte Iura altissimo, qui est inter Sequanos et Helvetios'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Itemque Dumnorigi Haeduo, fratri Diviciaci, qui eo tempore principatum in civitate obtinebat ac maxime plebi acceptus erat, ut idem conaretur persuadet eique filiam suam in matrimonium dat.
question: Cui Orgetorix filiam suam in matrimonium dedit?
question_en: To whom did Orgetorix give his daughter in marriage?
derivation: Relation fact anchored to Orgetorix; single named answer supported verbatim by 'eique filiam suam in matrimonium dat' (the antecedent being Dumnorix). Dumnorix is a major figure of Book 1; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Caesar, quod memoria tenebat L. Cassium consulem occisum exercitumque eius ab Helvetiis pulsum et sub iugum missum, concedendum non putabat.
question: Quem consulem Romanum Helvetii antea occiderant eiusque exercitum sub iugum miserant?
question_en: Which Roman consul had the Helvetii earlier killed, and sent his army under the yoke?
derivation: Historical name fact anchored to the Helvetii and a consul; single named answer supported verbatim. The defeat of L. Cassius (107 BC) is closed-book history echoed again in 1.12.

author: Caesar
source_text: Interea ea legione quam secum habebat militibusque, qui ex provincia convenerant, a lacu Lemanno, qui in flumen Rhodanum influit, ad montem Iuram, qui fines Sequanorum ab Helvetiis dividit, milia passuum XVIIII murum in altitudinem pedum sedecim fossamque perducit.
question: Quot milia passuum longum murum Caesar a lacu Lemanno ad montem Iuram perduxit?
question_en: How many miles long was the wall Caesar built from Lake Geneva to the Jura?
derivation: Number/engineering fact anchored to Caesar, Lake Leman, and the Jura; answer (XVIIII = 19) supported verbatim (the height being sixteen feet). Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Flumen est Arar, quod per fines Haeduorum et Sequanorum in Rhodanum influit, incredibili lenitate, ita ut oculis in utram partem fluat iudicari non possit.
question: In quod flumen Ararim influere Caesar scribit?
question_en: Into which river does Caesar write the Arar flows?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to the Arar (Saone); single answer supported verbatim by 'in Rhodanum influit'. Indirect statement (Ararim influere) governed by scribit; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Is pagus appellabatur Tigurinus; nam omnis civitas Helvetia in quattuor pagos divisa est. Hic pagus unus, cum domo exisset, patrum nostrorum memoria L. Cassium consulem interfecerat et eius exercitum sub iugum miserat.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur pagus Helvetius qui L. Cassium consulem interfecerat?
question_en: What was the name of the Helvetian canton that had killed the consul Lucius Cassius?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Helvetii and to Cassius; single named answer supported verbatim ('Is pagus appellabatur Tigurinus' + 'L. Cassium consulem interfecerat'). Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Legatos ad eum mittunt; cuius legationis Divico princeps fuit, qui bello Cassiano dux Helvetiorum fuerat.
question: Quis dux Helvetiorum bello Cassiano fuerat et postea legationi ad Caesarem missae praefuit?
question_en: Who had been the leader of the Helvetii in the Cassian war and later headed the embassy to Caesar?
derivation: Name fact doubly anchored (Helvetii, the Cassian war, Caesar); single named answer supported verbatim by 'Divico princeps fuit, qui bello Cassiano dux Helvetiorum fuerat'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Qui summo magistratui praeerat, quem vergobretum appellant Haedui, qui creatur annuus et vitae necisque in suos habet potestatem.
question: Quo nomine Haedui summum magistratum suum appellant?
question_en: By what name do the Haedui call their supreme magistrate?
derivation: Institution/custom fact anchored to the Haedui; single named answer supported verbatim by 'quem vergobretum appellant Haedui'. A distinctive named office (annual, with power of life and death); closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: A Bibracte, oppido Haeduorum longe maximo et copiosissimo, non amplius milibus passuum XVIII aberat.
question: Quod oppidum Haeduorum longe maximum et copiosissimum fuisse Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which town does Caesar write was by far the largest and richest of the Haedui?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Haedui; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Bibracte, oppido Haeduorum longe maximo et copiosissimo'. Indirect statement (fuisse) under scribit; the iconic Aeduan oppidum, closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: In castris Helvetiorum tabulae repertae sunt litteris Graecis confectae et ad Caesarem relatae, quibus in tabulis nominatim ratio confecta erat, qui numerus domo exisset eorum qui arma ferre possent, et item separatim, quot pueri, senes mulieresque.
question: Quibus litteris tabulae in castris Helvetiorum repertae confectae erant?
question_en: In what script were the tablets found in the camp of the Helvetii written?
derivation: A striking, much-cited fact anchored to the Helvetian camp; single answer supported verbatim by 'tabulae ... litteris Graecis confectae'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ariovistus, rex Germanorum, in eorum finibus consedisset tertiamque partem agri Sequani, qui esset optimus totius Galliae, occupavisset.
question: Quis erat rex Germanorum qui in finibus Sequanorum consedit?
question_en: Who was the king of the Germani who settled in the territory of the Sequani?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Germani and the Sequani; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Ariovistus, rex Germanorum, in eorum finibus consedisset'. Ariovistus is the central antagonist of Book 1; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Nuntiatum est ei Ariovistum cum suis omnibus copiis ad occupandum Vesontionem, quod est oppidum maximum Sequanorum, contendere.
question: Quod oppidum, Sequanorum maximum, Ariovistus occupare contendit?
question_en: Which town, the largest of the Sequani, did Ariovistus hasten to seize?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Sequani and Ariovistus; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vesontionem, quod est oppidum maximum Sequanorum'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Apud Germanos ea consuetudo esset ut matres familiae eorum sortibus et vaticinationibus declararent utrum proelium committi ex usu esset necne; eas ita dicere: non esse fas Germanos superare, si ante novam lunam proelio contendissent.
question: Ante quid Germanos vincere fas non esse matres familiae declarabant?
question_en: Before what did the German matrons declare it was not right (fas) for the Germani to win?
derivation: Ethnographic custom fact anchored to the Germani; short answer supported verbatim by 'non esse fas Germanos superare, si ante novam lunam proelio contendissent'. Distinctive and closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: crebri ad eum rumores adferebantur litterisque item Labieni certior fiebat omnes Belgas, quam tertiam esse Galliae partem dixeramus, contra populum Romanum coniurare obsidesque inter se dare.
question: Quam Galliae partem Belgas esse Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which part of Gaul does Caesar say the Belgae are?
derivation: The famous opening fact echoed from BG 1.1: the Belgae are the third of the three parts of Gaul. Anchored to the Belgae and Caesar; single answer supported verbatim by 'quam tertiam esse Galliae partem'. Indirect statement (Belgas esse partem) under scribit; closed-book staple of Latin geography.

author: Caesar
source_text: crebri ad eum rumores adferebantur litterisque item Labieni certior fiebat omnes Belgas, quam tertiam esse Galliae partem dixeramus, contra populum Romanum coniurare obsidesque inter se dare.
question: Contra quem populum omnes Belgas coniurare Caesar litteris Labieni certior factus est?
question_en: Against what people was Caesar informed, by letters from Labienus, that all the Belgae were conspiring?
derivation: The opening fact of Book II. Anchored to the Belgae, Labienus, and Caesar; single answer supported verbatim by 'omnes Belgas ... contra populum Romanum coniurare'. Indirect statement (Belgas coniurare) under certior factus est; closed-book.

author: Caesar
