question_en: How much right can anyone transfer to another, according to Ulpian's rule?
answer_en: No more than he himself would have.
derivation: The single most-cited regula iuris ('no one can transfer more right than he himself has'). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: In omnibus quidem, maxime tamen in iure aequitas spectanda est.
question: Ubi maxime aequitatem spectandam esse Paulus dicit?
question_en: Where above all does Paulus say equity must be regarded?
derivation: Paulus's famous maxim that equity must be regarded in everything, but most of all in law. Closed-book, anchored to Paulus + aequitas, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (aequitatem spectandam esse) governed by dicit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Non videntur qui errant consentire.
question: Quid de iis qui errant Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: What does Ulpian lay down as a rule about those who are in error?
answer_en: They are not regarded as consenting.
derivation: The famous maxim that error excludes consent (the basis of the doctrine of mistake). Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Qui tacet, non utique fatetur: sed tamen verum est eum non negare.
question: Quid de eo qui tacet Paulus regula tradit?
answer: Non utique fatetur, sed tamen verum est eum non negare.
question_en: What does Paulus lay down as a rule about one who keeps silent?
answer_en: He does not necessarily admit, but it is nonetheless true that he does not deny.
derivation: The famous maxim on the legal effect of silence (qui tacet consentire videtur is the later mangling; this is the precise Pauline rule). Closed-book, anchored to Paulus, answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Nemo damnum facit, nisi qui id fecit, quod facere ius non habet.
question: Quem solum damnum facere Paulus regula tradit?
answer: Eum qui id fecit quod facere ius non habet.
question_en: Who alone, by Paulus's rule, does (legally cognizable) damage?
answer_en: He who did what he had no right to do.
derivation: Paulus's famous maxim defining wrongful damage (a cornerstone of the lex Aquilia). Closed-book, anchored to Paulus + damnum, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (quem... facere) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Inpossibilium nulla obligatio est.
question: Quid de impossibilibus quoad obligationem Celsus regula tradit?
question_en: What does Celsus lay down as a rule about impossible things with respect to obligation?
answer_en: There is no obligation to (perform) the impossible.
derivation: Celsus's famous maxim that the impossible binds no one. Closed-book, anchored to Celsus, answer verbatim (note the source spelling 'Inpossibilium').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Omnis definitio in iure civili periculosa est: parum est enim, ut non subverti posset.
question: Qualem omnem definitionem in iure civili Iavolenus esse pronuntiat?
question_en: What does Javolenus declare every definition in the civil law to be?
derivation: Javolenus's celebrated warning against legal definitions ('every definition in civil law is dangerous'). Closed-book, anchored to Javolenus, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (definitionem... esse) governed by pronuntiat.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iure naturae aequum est neminem cum alterius detrimento et iniuria fieri locupletiorem.
question: Quid iure naturae aequum esse Pomponius tradit de locupletatione cum alterius detrimento?
answer: Neminem cum alterius detrimento et iniuria fieri locupletiorem.
question_en: What does Pomponius hand down as fair by the law of nature regarding enrichment at another's loss?
answer_en: That no one be made richer at another's loss and wrong.
derivation: The foundational maxim against unjust enrichment, the source of the modern principle. Closed-book, anchored to Pomponius, short answer present verbatim; acc.+inf. (neminem... fieri) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
locus: Justinian, Digesta 50.17.207 (Ulpianus 1 ad l. Iul. et Pap.)
source_text: Res iudicata pro veritate accipitur.
question: Pro qua re rem iudicatam accipi Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: As what, by Ulpian's rule, is a matter once adjudged taken?
derivation: The famous maxim that a final judgment is accepted as the truth (basis of res iudicata). Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim; acc.+inf. (rem iudicatam accipi) governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: C. Plinius Traiano imperatori. Tua quidem pietas, imperator sanctissime, optaverat, ut quam tardissime succederes patri; sed di immortales festinaverunt virtutes tuas ad gubernacula rei publicae quam susceperas admovere.
question: Ad quem imperatorem Plinius minor epistulas decimi libri suas direxit, a quo vicissim responsa accepit?
question_en: To which emperor did Pliny the Younger address his letters of the tenth book, and from whom he received replies in turn?
derivation: Addressee fact: the whole of Book X is the official correspondence between Pliny and the emperor Trajan; the salutations read 'C. Plinius Traiano imperatori' / 'Traianus Plinio', and 10.1 addresses Trajan as the new emperor who succeeded his (adoptive) father Nerva. Closed-book famous; entity-anchored to Pliny + Book X; single-name answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Rursus, cum transissem in orarias nauculas, contrariis ventis retentus aliquanto tardius quam speraveram, id est XV Kal. Octobres, Bithyniam intravi.
question: In quam provinciam, a Traiano legatus missus, Plinius minor ante diem quintum decimum Kalendas Octobres ingressus est?
question_en: Into which province, sent as Trajan's legate, did Pliny the Younger enter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October (17 September)?
derivation: Province fact: Pliny governed the province of Bithynia (and Pontus) as Trajan's special legate; he records 'Bithyniam intravi' on a.d. XV Kal. Oct. Answer supported verbatim. Closed-book famous (Pliny's governorship of Bithynia). The full province was Bithynia et Pontus (cf. 10.108 'Bithynas et Ponticas civitates', 10.112 'Bithyni et Pontici').

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cognitionibus de Christianis interfui numquam: ideo nescio quid et quatenus aut puniri soleat aut quaeri.
question: Cuius generis hominum cognitionibus se numquam interfuisse Plinius minor Traiano scribens fatetur?
question_en: At the trials of what kind of people does Pliny the Younger, writing to Trajan, confess he had never been present?
derivation: The famous letter 10.96, in which Pliny consults Trajan on how to handle Christians, opens by admitting he had never attended cognitiones de Christianis. Entity-anchored (Pliny + Christians), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Affirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem.
question: Cui Christiani, ut Plinio confessi sunt, stato die ante lucem coeuntes carmen quasi deo invicem dicere soliti erant?
question_en: To whom, as the Christians confessed to Pliny, were they accustomed to recite a hymn as to a god, gathering before dawn on a fixed day, in turn?
derivation: The celebrated description of early Christian worship: they met before dawn on a fixed day and sang 'carmen Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem'. Entity-anchored (Christians, Christ), short name answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Interrogavi ipsos an essent Christiani. Confitentes iterum ac tertio interrogavi supplicium minatus; perseverantes duci iussi.
question: Quid Plinius, supplicium minatus, de iis fieri iussit qui pertinaciter se Christianos esse confitebantur?
question_en: What did Pliny, having threatened punishment, order to be done to those who persistently confessed they were Christians?
answer_en: He ordered them led off (to execution).
derivation: Pliny's procedure: those who persisted in confessing (perseverantes) he ordered 'duci', i.e. led off to execution, holding that obstinacy must be punished. Entity-anchored (Pliny, Christians), short verbal answer supported verbatim.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Conquirendi non sunt; si deferantur et arguantur, puniendi sunt.
question: Quid Traianus, Plinio rescribens, de Christianis conquirendis statuit?
question_en: What did Trajan rule, in his reply to Pliny, about hunting out Christians?
answer_en: That they are not to be sought out.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Sine auctore vero propositi libelli in nullo crimine locum habere debent. Nam et pessimi exempli nec nostri saeculi est.
question: Quem locum Traianus libellis sine auctore propositis in criminibus tribuendum esse negavit?
answer: Nullum: in nullo crimine locum habere debent.
question_en: What standing did Trajan deny should be granted to anonymous written accusations in any charge?
answer_en: None: they are to have no place in any charge.
derivation: The second famous ruling of Trajan's rescript: anonymous denunciations ('sine auctore propositi libelli') are to have no place in any charge, being a bad precedent unworthy of the age. Entity-anchored (Trajan), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cautum est, domine, Pompeia lege quae Bithynis data est, ne quis capiat magistratum neve sit in senatu minor annorum triginta.
question: Minor quot annorum, ex lege Pompeia Bithynis data, magistratum capere aut in senatu esse non poterat?
question_en: Younger than how many years, by the lex Pompeia given to the Bithynians, could a man not hold a magistracy or sit in the senate?

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Tu, domine, dispice an instituendum putes collegium fabrorum dumtaxat hominum CL.
question: Quod collegium Plinius, post vastissimum Nicomediae incendium, instituendum Traiano proposuit?
question_en: What guild did Pliny propose to Trajan should be established after a devastating fire at Nicomedia?
answer_en: A guild of workmen (a fire brigade, collegium fabrorum).

Entity-anchored (Pliny, Nicomedia), short answer; a recognizable exchange in the history of Roman associations.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Tuo tamen desiderio subscripsi et dedisse me ius trium liberorum Suetonio Tranquillo ea condicione, qua assuevi, referri in commentarios meos iussi.
question: Cui viro erudito, postea 'De vita Caesarum' auctori, Plinius a Traiano ius trium liberorum impetravit?

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: In aquae ductum, domine, Nicomedenses impenderunt HS XXX CCCXVIII, qui imperfectus adhuc omissus, destructus etiam est; rursus in alium ductum erogata sunt CC.
question: Quae civitas, ut Plinius Traiano scribit, magnam pecuniam in aquae ductus imperfectos frustra erogaverat?
question_en: Which city, as Pliny writes to Trajan, had wastefully spent a great sum of money on unfinished aqueducts?

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: C. Plinius Tacito suo s. Petis ut tibi avunculi mei exitum scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis.
question: Quis a Plinio minore petivit ut avunculi sui exitum scriberet, quo verius posteris traderetur?
question_en: Who asked Pliny the Younger to write an account of his uncle's death, so that it could be handed down to posterity more truly?

author: Pliny the Younger

question: Quo gradu necessitudinis vir ille, cuius mortem Plinius minor ad Tacitum perscripsit, scriptori coniunctus erat?

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nonum Kal. Septembres hora fere septima mater mea indicat ei apparere nubem inusitata et magnitudine et specie.
question: Quo die mater Plinii minoris fratri suo nubem inusitatam apparere indicavit?

answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August).
derivation: Date fact: 'Nonum Kal. Septembres' = a.d. IX Kal. Sept. = 24 August (AD 79), the traditional date of the eruption. The 'mater mea' (Pliny the Younger's mother) was sister of Pliny the Elder, hence 'fratri suo.' Entity-anchored, date answer; closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit. Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur.
question: Cui arbori potissimum similem fuisse nubem e Vesuvio ortam Plinius scribit?

derivation: Famous simile: the eruption column shaped 'non alia magis arbor quam pinus' — a long trunk spreading into branches at the top (umbrella pine). Translatable (a tree, not wordplay), entity-anchored, short answer; one of the best-known images in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Egrediebatur domo; accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci imminenti periculo exterritae — nam villa eius subiacebat, nec ulla nisi navibus fuga -: ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.

derivation: Named appeal: 'accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci ... ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.' Rectina's message turned his scientific reconnaissance into a rescue mission. Entity-anchored named person, single answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret, mox gubernatori ut ita faceret monenti 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.'

derivation: Named destination: 'Pomponianum pete' — he sailed on to join Pomponianus (at Stabiae). Entity-anchored named person; short answer; the maxim 'fortes fortuna iuvat' anchors the moment.

source_text: 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.' Stabiis erat diremptus sinu medio — nam sensim circumactis curvatisque litoribus mare infunditur.

author: Pliny the Younger

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Hic situs est Rufus, pulso qui Vindice quondam imperium asseruit non sibi sed patriae.

derivation: Historical fact: in letter 6.10 about Verginius Rufus's tomb, his self-composed epitaph reads 'pulso ... Vindice' — having suppressed the revolt of Vindex (AD 68) he claimed empire 'not for himself but for the fatherland.' Entity-anchored, single-name answer; closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Accusavi Marium Priscum, qui lege repetundarum damnatus utebatur clementia legis, cuius severitatem immanitate criminum excesserat; relegatus est.

derivation: First-person fact: 'Accusavi Marium Priscum ... lege repetundarum damnatus ... relegatus est.' The celebrated extortion trial of Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa. Entity-anchored to Pliny and Marius Priscus; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder

answer_en: The shape of a globe (a sphere).

author: Pliny the Elder

answer_en: In the space of twenty-four hours.

author: Pliny the Elder

derivation: The seven 'wandering stars' (the classical planetae, counting the sun and moon). Entity-anchored to the planets set between earth and heaven; single numeric answer (seven) supported verbatim by septem sidera... errantia. Closed-book: the seven planets are a fixture of ancient astronomy.

question: Quod ex septem errantibus sideribus medium ferri et caeli rectorem esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Which of the seven wandering stars does Pliny say moves in the middle and is the ruler of the heaven?
derivation: The sun's central place among the seven planets and its role as 'ruler.' Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (the sun) supported verbatim by eorum medius sol fertur... caelique rector. Indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: summum esse quod vocant Saturni sidus ideoque minimum videri et maximo ambire circulo ac tricesimo anno ad brevissima sedis suae principia regredi certum est.

question_en: Which wandering star does Pliny say is both the highest and returns to the beginning of its course in the thirtieth year?
derivation: Saturn is the outermost/highest of the planets and has the longest period, returning in the thirtieth year. Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (Saturn) supported verbatim by summum esse quod vocant Saturni sidus... tricesimo anno... regredi. author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Sed omnium admirationem vincit novissimum sidus, terris familiarissimum et in tenebrarum remedium ab natura apertum, lunae.

question_en: Which of the wandering stars does Pliny say is the lowest, that is, nearest to the earth?
derivation: The moon is the lowest (novissimum) of the seven planets and 'most familiar to the lands' (nearest), hence the smallest, fastest orbit (2.44). Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (the moon) supported verbatim by novissimum sidus, terris familiarissimum... lunae. Closed-book: the moon as the nearest celestial body is basic ancient astronomy.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: solis fulgore, ut reliqua siderum, regi, siquidem in totum mutuata ab eo luce fulgere, qualem in repercussu aquae volitare conspicimus.
question: Unde lunam lumen suum habere Plinius tradit?
question_en: From where does Pliny say the moon has its light?
answer_en: From the sun, with borrowed light.
derivation: The moon shines not by its own light but with light wholly borrowed from the sun. Entity-anchored to the moon; short answer (from the sun) supported verbatim by solis fulgore... regi, siquidem in totum mutuata ab eo luce fulgere. Indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book: that the moon's light is reflected sunlight is a well-known ancient finding.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: quippe manifestum est solem interventu lunae occultari lunamque terrae obiectu ac vices reddi, eosdem solis radios luna interpositu suo auferente terrae terraque lunae.

answer: Solem interventu lunae, lunam obiectu terrae.
question_en: Through the interposition of what does Pliny say the sun is eclipsed, and through the obstruction of what the moon?
answer_en: The sun by the interposition of the moon, the moon by the obstruction (shadow) of the earth.
derivation: The mechanism of eclipses: a solar eclipse is the sun hidden by the moon coming between, a lunar eclipse is the moon falling into the earth's shadow/obstruction. Closed-book: the cause of eclipses is a canonical ancient fact.

author: Pliny the Elder

answer_en: Nothing other than the shadow of the earth.
derivation: Night defined as nothing other than the earth's shadow (a consequence of the eclipse/shadow geometry). Entity-anchored to night and the earth; short answer supported verbatim by neque aliud esse noctem quam terrae umbram. Indirect statement governed by adfirmat. Closed-book and memorable.

derivation: The famous prediction of a solar eclipse by Thales of Miletus (in the reign of Alyattes). author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Infra solem ambit ingens sidus appellatum Veneris, alterno meatu vagum ipsisque cognominibus aemulum solis ac lunae. praeveniens quippe et ante matutinum exoriens luciferi nomen accepit ut sol alter diemque maturans, contra ab occasu refulgens nuncupatur vesper ut prorogans lucem vicemve lunae reddens.

author: Pliny the Elder

author: Pliny the Elder

answer_en: Into three parts: Europe, Asia, and Africa.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hiberus amnis, navigabili commercio dives, ortus in Cantabris haut procul oppido Iuliobrica, per CCCCL p. fluens, navium per CCLX a Vareia oppido capax, quem propter universam Hispaniam Graeci appellavere Hiberiam.
question: A quo flumine Graeci universam Hispaniam Hiberiam appellaverunt secundum Plinium?
question_en: After which river did the Greeks name all of Spain 'Iberia,' according to Pliny?
derivation: Etymology of Iberia from the river Hiberus (Ebro). Entity-anchored (Spain, the Greeks, the river); single named answer supported verbatim by quem propter ... Graeci appellavere Hiberiam. Closed-book, recognizable geographic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Pyrenaei montes Hispanias Galliasque disterminant promunturiis in duo diversa maria proiectis.
question: Qui montes Hispanias Galliasque inter se disterminant secundum Plinium?
question_en: Which mountains separate the Spains from the Gauls, according to Pliny?
derivation: Boundary fact: the Pyrenees divide Spain from Gaul. Two named regions, one mountain-range answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, textbook geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: praefari necessarium est auctorem nos Divum Augustum secuturos discriptionemque ab eo factam Italiae totius in regiones XI.
question: In quot regiones Divus Augustus Italiam totam discripsisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Into how many regions is the Deified Augustus said by Pliny to have divided all of Italy?
derivation: The famous Augustan division of Italy into eleven regiones, which structures the rest of the book. Anchored to Augustus + Italy; single number answer (XI) supported verbatim. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Augustus discripsisse traditur). Closed-book, attributed.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Est ergo folio maxime querno adsimulata, multo proceritate amplior quam latitudine.
question: Cui folio figuram Italiae maxime adsimilari Plinius scribit?
question_en: To which leaf does Pliny say the shape of Italy is most likened?
derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of Italy (an oak leaf). Subject (Italia) is the running topic; the question supplies it, making it decontextualizable. Short answer supported verbatim by folio querno adsimulata. Indirect statement governed by scribit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: conplexa montes septem. ipsa dividitur in regiones XIIII, compita Larum CCLXV.
question: In quot regiones ipsa urbs Roma divisa est secundum Plinium?
question_en: Into how many regions is the city of Rome itself divided, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Augustan fourteen regiones of the city of Rome (distinct from the eleven regiones of Italy). Anchored to Rome; single number answer (XIV) supported verbatim. Question names urbs Roma so the source's ipsa is unambiguous. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tiberis, ante Thyberis appellatus et prius Albula, e media fere longitudine Appennini finibus Arretinorum profluit.
question: Quo nomine Tiberis amnis antiquissime appellatus esse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: By what name does Pliny say the river Tiber was called in earliest times?
derivation: The Tiber's oldest name. The text gives prius Albula (earlier than both Tiberis and Thyberis), so Albula is the earliest. Entity-anchored to the Tiber, single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a recurring antiquarian fact in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: fluvius Rubico, quondam finis Italiae.
question: Qui fluvius quondam finis Italiae fuisse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which river does Pliny say was once the boundary of Italy?
derivation: The Rubicon as the former boundary of Italy (proper). Single named-river answer supported verbatim by Rubico, quondam finis Italiae. Closed-book and iconic (Caesar's crossing).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hirpinorum colonia una Beneventum auspicatius mutato nomine, quae quondam appellata Maleventum.
question: Quo nomine colonia Beneventum, ante nominis mutationem, quondam appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name was the colony of Beneventum formerly called, before its name was changed, according to Pliny?
derivation: The renaming of Maleventum to the more auspicious Beneventum. Anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, frequently cited etymological/onomastic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: oppidum Paestum, Graecis Posidonia appellatum, sinus Paestanus.
question: Quo nomine oppidum Paestum a Graecis appellatum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By what name do the Greeks call the town of Paestum, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of Paestum. Entity-anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (the Greek colony Poseidonia).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Padus, e gremio Vesuli montis celsissimum in cacumen Alpium elati finibus Ligurum Bagiennorum visendo fonte profluens condensque se cuniculo et in Forovibiensium agro iterum exoriens, nullo amnium claritate inferior, Graecis dictus Eridanus ac poena Phaethontis inlustratus.
question: Quo nomine Padus amnis a Graecis dictus esse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: By what name was the river Padus (Po) called by the Greeks, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of the Po, tied to the myth of Phaethon. Anchored to the Padus; single-name answer supported verbatim by Graecis dictus Eridanus. Closed-book, well-known.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Verum ante omnes claritate Sicilia, Sicania Thucydidi dicta, Trinacria pluribus aut Trinacia a triangula specie.
question: Quo nomine Sicilia a plerisque ob triangulam speciem appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name is Sicily called by most people on account of its triangular shape, according to Pliny?
derivation: The name Trinacria for triangular Sicily. Anchored to Sicily; single-name answer supported verbatim by Trinacria ... a triangula specie. Closed-book, iconic (the island's three-cornered shape).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: in hoc tractu interierunt Boi, quorum tribus CXII fuisse auctor est Cato, item Senones, qui ceperunt Romam.
question: Quae Gallorum gens Romam cepisse a Plinio memoratur?
question_en: Which Gallic people does Pliny record as having captured Rome?
derivation: Attributes the sack of Rome to the Senones. Anchored to Rome + the Gauls; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Senones, qui ceperunt Romam. Closed-book (Brennus' Gauls, 390 BC).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ex quibus Laevi et Marici condidere Ticinum non procul a Pado, sicut Boi Transalpibus profecti Laudem Pompeiam, Insubres Mediolanum.
question: Quae gens Mediolanum condidisse secundum Plinium traditur?
question_en: Which people is said by Pliny to have founded Mediolanum (Milan)?
derivation: Founder fact: the Insubres founded Mediolanum (the verb condidere governs the list, sicut ... Insubres Mediolanum). Anchored to the city; single named-people answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (Milan).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Molossi, apud quos Dodonaei Iovis templum oraculo inlustre
question: Apud quam Epiri gentem templum Dodonaei Iovis, oraculo inlustre, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Among which people of Epirus does Pliny say the temple of Dodonaean Jupiter, famous for its oracle, is located?
derivation: The famous oracle and temple of Dodonaean Jupiter lies among the Molossi of Epirus. Anchored to Dodona plus Jupiter's oracle; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Molossi, apud quos Dodonaei Iovis templum oraculo inlustre. Closed-book: Dodona is among the most famous Greek oracles. Indirect statement templum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: a quo VII p. introrsus liberum oppidum Delphi sub monte Parnaso, clarissimi in terris oraculi Apollinis.
question: Sub quo monte oppidum Delphi, cum clarissimo Apollinis oraculo, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Under which mountain does Pliny say the town of Delphi, with its most famous oracle of Apollo, is situated?
derivation: The location of Delphi, seat of the most famous oracle of Apollo, beneath Mount Parnassus. Anchored to Delphi plus Apollo's oracle; single named-mountain answer supported verbatim by Delphi sub monte Parnaso. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement oppidum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Peloponnesus, Apia antea appellata et Pelasgia, paeninsula haut ulli terrae nobilitate postferenda, inter duo maria Aegeum et Ionium, platani folio similis propter angulosos recessus, circuitu DLXIII p. colligit auctore Isidoro.
question: Cui folio Peloponnesum propter angulosos recessus similem esse Plinius scribit?
question_en: To which leaf does Pliny say the Peloponnese is similar, on account of its angular indentations?
derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of the Peloponnese (a plane-tree leaf), paralleling the oak-leaf simile for Italy in Book III. Anchored to the Peloponnese; short answer (folio platani) supported verbatim by platani folio similis. Indirect statement Peloponnesum similem esse governed by scribit; closed-book, recognizable geographic image.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: intus delubrum Olympii Iovis, ludorum claritate fastos Graeciae complexum, Pisaeorum quondam oppidum, praefluente Alpheo amne.
question: Quo amne praefluente delubrum Olympii Iovis, ludorum claritate nobile, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By which river flowing past does Pliny say the temple of Olympian Jupiter, famous for its games, stands?
derivation: Olympia, site of the temple of Olympian Jupiter and the Olympic games, lies by the river Alpheus. Anchored to Olympian Jupiter plus the games; single named-river answer supported verbatim by praefluente Alpheo amne. Closed-book, iconic (the Alpheus of Olympia). Ablative absolute in question; indirect statement delubrum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: et ante cunctos claritate Penius, ortos iuxta Gomphos interque Ossam et Olympum nemorosa convalle defluens D stadiis, dimidio eius spatii navigabilis.
question: Inter quos montes Penium amnem nemorosa convalle defluere Plinius tradit?
question_en: Between which two mountains does Pliny say the river Peneus flows through a wooded valley?
derivation: The river Peneus runs through a wooded valley (the Vale of Tempe) between Mounts Ossa and Olympus in Thessaly. Anchored to the Peneus; two named mountains as answer, supported verbatim by interque Ossam et Olympum nemorosa convalle defluens. Closed-book, iconic (Tempe; the two great mountains of Thessaly). Indirect statement Penium defluere governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: fretum, quo montem Atho Xerxes Persarum rex continenti abscidit in longitudinem passuum MD.
question: Qui Persarum rex montem Atho freto a continenti abscidisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Which king of the Persians is said by Pliny to have cut Mount Athos off from the mainland by a channel?
derivation: Xerxes' famous canal severing Mount Athos from the mainland. Anchored to Mount Athos plus the Persian king; single named-person answer supported verbatim by Xerxes Persarum rex ... abscidit. Closed-book, iconic engineering feat. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Xerxes abscidisse traditur).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: haec eadem est Macedonia, cuius uno die Paulus Aemilius imperator noster LXII urbes direptas vendidit.
question: Quot Macedoniae urbes Paulum Aemilium uno die direptas vendidisse Plinius tradit?
question_en: How many cities of Macedonia does Pliny say Paulus Aemilius sold as plunder in a single day?
derivation: The striking claim that Aemilius Paulus sold sixty-two plundered Macedonian cities in one day (after Pydna, 167 BC). Anchored to Paulus Aemilius plus Macedonia; single number answer (LXII) supported verbatim. Indirect statement Paulum Aemilium vendidisse governed by tradit. Closed-book historical fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: promunturium Chryseon Ceras, in quo oppidum Byzantium liberae condicionis, antea Lygos dictum;
question: Quo nomine oppidum Byzantium antea appellatum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By what name does Pliny say the town of Byzantium was formerly called?
derivation: The former name of Byzantium (Lygos). Anchored to Byzantium; single-name answer supported verbatim by Byzantium ... antea Lygos dictum. Closed-book, iconic city. Indirect statement oppidum appellatum esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Ipsa Creta, altero latere ad austrum, altero ad septentrionem versa, inter ortum occasumque porrigitur centum urbium clara fama.
question: Quot urbium fama Cretam insulam claram esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: For the fame of how many cities does Pliny say the island of Crete is renowned?
derivation: Crete's proverbial fame as the island of a hundred cities (the Homeric hekatompolis). Anchored to Crete; single number answer (centum) supported verbatim by centum urbium clara fama. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement Cretam claram esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: a promunturio Geraesto circa Delum in orbem sitae, unde et nomen traxere, Cyclades.
question: Circa quam insulam Cycladas in orbem sitas esse Plinius tradit, unde nomen traxerint?
question_en: Around which island does Pliny say the Cyclades are set in a circle, whence they took their name?
derivation: The etymology of the Cyclades: they lie in a ring around Delos. Anchored to the Cyclades plus Delos; single named-island answer supported verbatim by circa Delum in orbem sitae ... Cyclades. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement Cycladas sitas esse governed by tradit; embedded indirect question traxerint.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Paros cum oppido, ab Delo XXXVIII, marmore nobilis, quam primo Platean, postea Minoida vocarunt.
question: Qua re insula Paros apud Plinium nobilis est?
question_en: For what is the island of Paros notable, according to Pliny?
derivation: Paros' fame for its marble (Parian marble). Anchored to Paros; single short answer (marmore, ablative of respect) supported verbatim by Paros ... marmore nobilis. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: primas angustias Hellespontum vocant; hac Xerxes Persarum rex constrato in navibus ponte duxit exercitum.
question: Per quas angustias Xerxes Persarum rex constrato in navibus ponte exercitum duxisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Across which strait is Xerxes, king of the Persians, said by Pliny to have led his army over a bridge built on ships?
derivation: Xerxes' bridge of boats across the Hellespont. Anchored to Xerxes; single named-strait answer supported verbatim by Hellespontum ... Xerxes ... constrato in navibus ponte duxit exercitum. Closed-book, iconic. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Xerxes duxisse traditur). Distinct from the Athos pair (different deed, different answer).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: dein vastum mare Pontus Euxinus, qui quondam Axenus, longe refugientes occupat terras magnoque litorum flexu retro curvatus in cornua ab iis utrimque porrigitur, ut sit plane arcus Scythici forma.
question: Cuius generis arcus formam Pontum Euxinum habere Plinius scribit?
question_en: The shape of what kind of bow does Pliny write that the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus) has?
derivation: Pliny's vivid simile that the Black Sea, curved into two horns, has exactly the shape of a Scythian bow. Anchored to the Pontus Euxinus; short answer (a Scythian bow) supported verbatim by ut sit plane arcus Scythici forma. Closed-book, recognizable geographic image. Indirect statement Pontum habere governed by scribit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Albion ipsi nomen fuit, cum Britanniae vocarentur omnes de quibus mox paulo dicemus.
question: Quod nomen insulae Britanniae ipsi antea fuisse Plinius tradit?
question_en: What name does Pliny say the island of Britain itself formerly bore?
derivation: The old name of the island of Britain (Albion), when the plural Britanniae denoted the whole island-group. Anchored to Britain; single-name answer supported verbatim by Albion ipsi nomen fuit. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement nomen fuisse governed by tradit; insulae Britanniae ipsi is dative of possession.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ultima omnium quae memorantur Tyle, in qua solstitio nullas esse noctes indicavimus, cancri signum sole transeunte, nullosque contra per brumam dies.
question: In qua insula, omnium ultima, solstitio nullas esse noctes Plinius indicat?
question_en: On which island, the most remote of all, does Pliny indicate that there are no nights at the summer solstice?
derivation: Thule, the most remote island, where there is no night at the summer solstice. Pinned by the defining property (no nights at the solstice; the northernmost land), yielding the famous Thule. Supported verbatim by Tyle, in qua solstitio nullas esse noctes. Closed-book, iconic (ultima Thule). Indirect statement nullas esse noctes governed by indicat.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tagus auriferis harenis celebratur.
question: Quibus harenis Tagus amnis apud Plinium celebratur?
question_en: For what kind of sands is the river Tagus celebrated, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Tagus' fame for gold-bearing sands. Anchored to the Tagus; short answer (auriferae harenae, ablative) supported verbatim by Tagus auriferis harenis celebratur. Closed-book, iconic (the gold of the Tagus).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Africam Graeci Libyam appellavere et mare ante eam Libycum.
question: Quo nomine Africa a Graecis appellata esse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: By what name does Pliny say Africa was called by the Greeks?
derivation: Opening fact of the book: the Greek name for Africa is Libya. Anchored to Africa + the Greeks; single named answer supported verbatim by Africam Graeci Libyam appellavere. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Africa appellata esse) governed by dicitur; closed-book because Libya as the Greek term for Africa is a commonplace of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: multo tamen magis Autololum gente, per quam iter est ad montem Africae vel fabulosissimum Atlantem.
question: Quem montem Plinius 'montem Africae vel fabulosissimum' nominat?
question_en: Which mountain does Pliny call 'the mountain of Africa, and the most fabulous'?
derivation: Identifies Atlas as the iconic mountain of Africa. Single named-mountain answer supported verbatim by montem Africae vel fabulosissimum Atlantem; nominat takes the double accusative (quem montem ... Atlantem). Closed-book: Mount Atlas is among the best-known landmarks of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ita se findente Nilo, ut triquetram terrae figuram efficiat, ideoque multi Graecae litterae vocabulo Delta appellavere Aegyptum.
question: Quo Graecae litterae vocabulo multi Aegyptum appellaverunt, ob triquetram figuram quam Nilus se findens efficit, secundum Plinium?
question_en: By the name of which Greek letter did many call Egypt, on account of the triangular shape that the Nile forms by splitting, according to Pliny?
answer_en: By the name of the letter Delta.
derivation: Egypt named 'Delta' from the Greek letter because the Nile, splitting, makes a triangular shape. Anchored to Egypt + the Nile; single answer supported verbatim by Graecae litterae vocabulo Delta appellavere Aegyptum. Closed-book and iconic (the Nile Delta).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: auctus per puteos mensurae notis deprehenduntur. iustum incrementum est cubitorum XVI.
question: Quot cubitorum esse iustum Nili incrementum Plinius tradit?
question_en: Of how many cubits does Pliny say the proper rise of the Nile is?
derivation: The famous ideal flood-height of the Nile, sixteen cubits. Anchored to the Nile; single number answer supported verbatim by iustum incrementum est cubitorum XVI. Indirect statement (incrementum esse) governed by tradit; closed-book (the Nilometer's sixteen cubits).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: inde LXII p. abest Memphis, quondam arx Aegypti regum.
question: Quod oppidum Aegypti quondam arx regum fuisse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which Egyptian town does Pliny say was once the citadel of the kings?
derivation: Memphis as the ancient royal seat of Egypt. Anchored to Egypt + its kings; single-name answer supported verbatim by Memphis, quondam arx Aegypti regum. Nominativus cum infinitivo (oppidum ... arx fuisse) governed by dicitur; closed-book and recognizable.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Diospolis Magna, eadem Thebe portarum centum nobilis fama.
question: Quae urbs Aegypti, eadem Diospolis Magna, centum portarum fama nobilis est secundum Plinium?
question_en: Which Egyptian city, also called Diospolis Magna, is famed for its hundred gates, according to Pliny?
derivation: The hundred-gated Thebes (Diospolis Magna). Anchored to Egypt + the alternate name Diospolis Magna; single-name answer supported verbatim by Thebe portarum centum nobilis fama. Closed-book: the hekatompylos Thebes is a Homeric commonplace.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Sed iure laudetur in litore Aegyptii maris Alexandria, a Magno Alexandro condita in Africae parte ab ostio Canopico XII p. iuxta Mareotim lacum, qui locus antea Rhacotes nominabatur.
question: A quo Alexandria in Aegypto condita esse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: By whom does Pliny say Alexandria in Egypt was founded?
derivation: Founder fact: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria. Anchored to the city; single named-founder answer (ablative of agent) supported verbatim by Alexandria, a Magno Alexandro condita. Nominativus cum infinitivo governed by traditur; closed-book and iconic.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: altera iuncta ponte Alexandriae, colonia Caesaris dictatoris, Pharos, quondam diei navigatione distans ab Aegypto, nunc e turri nocturnis ignibus cursum navium regens.
question: Quae insula apud Alexandriam e turri nocturnis ignibus cursum navium regere a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which island by Alexandria does Pliny say guides ships' course from a tower by nighttime fires?
derivation: The lighthouse island of Pharos at Alexandria. Anchored to Alexandria; single-name answer supported verbatim by Pharos ... e turri nocturnis ignibus cursum navium regens. Nominativus cum infinitivo governed by dicitur; closed-book (the Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ac magis etiamnum meridiana Babylonia, eadem Mesopotamia inter Euphraten et Tigrin.
question: Inter quae duo flumina regionem Mesopotamiam sitam esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Between which two rivers does Pliny say the region of Mesopotamia lies?
answer_en: Between the Euphrates and the Tigris.
derivation: Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Anchored to the named region; two-river answer supported verbatim by Mesopotamia inter Euphraten et Tigrin. Indirect statement (Mesopotamiam sitam esse) governed by tradit; closed-book (the very meaning of 'Mesopotamia').

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: in qua fuere Hierosolyma, longe clarissima urbium orientis, non Iudaeae modo.
question: Quae urbs Iudaeae a Plinio 'longe clarissima urbium orientis' appellatur?
question_en: Which city of Judaea does Pliny call 'by far the most famous of the cities of the East'?
derivation: Pliny's superlative for Jerusalem, longe clarissima urbium orientis. Anchored to Judaea; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and iconic; passive appellatur keeps the 'according to Pliny' frame.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Ab occidente litora Esseni fugiunt usque qua nocent, gens sola et in toto orbe praeter ceteras mira, sine ulla femina, omni venere abdicata, sine pecunia, socia palmarum.
question: Quae gens ad occidentale latus lacus Asphaltitae sine ulla femina degere a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Which people does Pliny record as living on the western side of the Dead Sea (Lake Asphaltites) without any woman?
derivation: Pliny's famous notice placing the celibate Esseni on the western shore of the Dead Sea. Anchored to the lake + the womanless people; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Esseni ... sine ulla femina. Nominativus cum infinitivo governed by traditur; closed-book (the Essenes).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tyros, quondam insula praealto mari DCC passibus divisa, nunc vero Alexandri oppugnantis operibus continens; olim partu clara, urbibus genitis Lepti, Utica et illa aemula terrarumque orbis avida Carthagine, etiam Gadibus extra orbem conditis.
question: Cuius urbis Phoeniciae partu Carthaginem, Uticam, Gades genitas esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By the offspring of which Phoenician city does Pliny say Carthage, Utica, and Gades were founded?
derivation: Tyre as the Phoenician mother-city of Carthage (and Utica and Gades). Anchored to Carthage et al.; single-name answer (genitive) supported verbatim by Tyros ... urbibus genitis ... Carthagine ... Gadibus. Indirect statement governed by tradit; closed-book (Carthage's Tyrian foundation).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Arabia supra dicta habet oppida Edessam, quae quondam Antiochia dicebatur, Callirhoem, a fonte nominatam, Carrhas, Crassi clade nobile.
question: Quod oppidum a Plinio 'Crassi clade nobile' dicitur?
question_en: Which town does Pliny call 'famous for the defeat of Crassus'?
derivation: Carrhae as the site famous for Crassus' disaster. Anchored to Crassus; single-name answer supported verbatim by Carrhas, Crassi clade nobile. Closed-book and iconic (the Battle of Carrhae, 53 BC).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Palmyra, urbs nobilis situ, divitiis soli et aquis amoenis, vasto undique ambitu haernis includit agros ac, velut terris exempta a rerum natura, privata sorte inter duo imperia summa Romanorum Parthorumque est, prima in discordia semper utrimque cura.
question: Inter quae duo summa imperia urbem Palmyram sitam esse Plinius scribit?
question_en: Between which two great empires does Pliny say the city of Palmyra is situated?
answer_en: Between the empires of the Romans and the Parthians.
derivation: Palmyra lies between the two great empires of Rome and Parthia. Anchored to the named city; two-empire answer supported verbatim by inter duo imperia summa Romanorum Parthorumque est. Indirect statement (Palmyram sitam esse) governed by scribit; closed-book and recognizable.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Sed pulcherrima est libera Rhodos, circuitu CXXV aut, si potius Isidoro credimus, CIII, habitata urbibus Lindo, Camiro, Ialyso, nunc Rhodo.

author: Senatus Romanus

author: Senatus Romanus

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Haice utei in coventionid exdeicatis ne minus trinum noundinum, senatuosque sententiam utei scientes esetis.

answer_en: For a trinum nundinum — not less than three successive market-days.

Supported verbatim; the nundinum is a Roman institution, so the fact is culturally salient and translatable as a span of market-days.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Sei ques esent, quei arvorsum ead fecisent, quam suprad scriptum est, eeis rem caputalem faciendam censuere.
question: Quae poena constituta est eis, qui contra senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus fecissent?
question_en: What penalty was laid down for those who acted contrary to the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus?
answer_en: A capital charge (it was made a capital offense).
derivation: The sanction clause: 'eeis rem caputalem faciendam censuere' — proceedings against violators are to be capital. Answer 'res capitalis' is the archaic caputalem normalized; supported verbatim. With the mass executions Livy 39.18 reports, the capital penalty is the decree's most notorious feature.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: atque utei hoce in tabolam ahenam inceideretis, ita senatus aiquom censuit, uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit.
question: In quam tabulam senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus incidi senatus aequum censuit?
question_en: Onto what kind of tablet did the senate deem it right that the decree about the Bacchanalia be engraved?
derivation: The engraving order: 'in tabolam ahenam inceideretis' — cut this onto a bronze tablet. Answer supported verbatim (archaic tabolam ahenam = tabulam aeneam); the surviving Tiriolo bronze is that very object, which is precisely why the document is famous.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: atque utei hoce in tabolam ahenam inceideretis, ita senatus aiquom censuit, uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit.
question: Ubi tabulam aeneam senatus consulti de Bacchanalibus figi oportuit?
question_en: Where was the bronze tablet of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus to be posted?
answer_en: Where it could most easily be known (read).
derivation: The posting order: 'uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit' — fasten it up where it can most easily be known. The brief purpose-phrase is the answer, normalized from one of the most-quoted archaic phrases of the inscription; supported verbatim.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Atque utei ea Bacanalia, sei qua sunt, exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est, ita utei suprad scriptum est, in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt, faciatis utei dismota sient.
question: Intra quot dies, postquam tabellae datae essent, Bacchanalia ex senatus consulto dimovenda erant?
question_en: Within how many days after the tablets were delivered were the Bacchanalia to be dismantled under the senatus consultum?
derivation: The demolition clause: existing Bacchanalia (shrines) are to be dismantled 'in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt' — within ten days of the tablets' delivery. Single number answer supported verbatim; the ten-day deadline is a standard quoted detail of the decree.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Atque utei ea Bacanalia, sei qua sunt, exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est, ita utei suprad scriptum est, in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt, faciatis utei dismota sient.
question: Quid unum excipiebatur, cum Bacchanalia ex senatus consulto dimoveri iuberentur?
question_en: What one thing was excepted when the Bacchanalia were ordered dismantled under the senatus consultum?
answer_en: Anything sacred that was there (sacred objects were exempt from the demolition).
derivation: The exception to demolition: 'exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est' — except insofar as anything sacred is there. Brief answer supported verbatim; the scrupulous exemption of consecrated objects even while destroying the shrines is a noted, characteristically Roman feature of the decree.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: In agro Teurano.
question: Ad quem agrum pertinet exemplum aeneum senatus consulti de Bacchanalibus, quod adhuc exstat?
question_en: To which territory does the still-extant bronze copy of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus pertain?
answer_en: To the ager Teuranus (in Bruttium; the bronze was found at modern Tiriolo).
derivation: The subscription 'In agro Teurano' localizes this copy to the ager Teuranus in Bruttium, where the bronze was found (Tiriolo, 1640). Named-place answer supported verbatim; the findspot is part of the document's fame as one of the oldest surviving Latin inscriptions.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Natus est Augustus M. Tullio Cicerone C. Antonio conss. XIIII. Kal. Octob., paulo ante solis exortum, regione Palati, ad Capita bubulo, ubi nunc sacrarium habet, aliquanto post quam excessit constitutum.
question: Quibus consulibus natum esse Augustum Suetonius tradit?
answer: M. Tullio Cicerone et C. Antonio.
question_en: In whose consulship does Suetonius say Augustus was born?
answer_en: When Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius were consuls.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

derivation: Atia was daughter of Iulia, sister of C. Caesar, making Augustus the dictator's great-nephew (and adopted heir). Supported by 'Iulia, sorore C. Caesaris.' Entity-anchored, single answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: superstitibus liberis Octavia maiore, quam ex Ancharia, et Octavia minore item Augusto, quos ex Atia tulerat.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Infanti cognomen Thurino inditum est, in memoriam maiorum originis.

derivation: His original childhood cognomen, before 'Augustus'. Indirect statement (inditum esse) under tradit; supported by 'cognomen Thurino inditum est.' Closed-book naming fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Postea Gai Caesaris et deinde Augusti cognomen assumpsit, alterum testamento maioris avunculi, alterum Munati Planci sententia, cum, quibusdam censentibus Romulum appellari oportere quasi et ipsum conditorem urbis, praevaluisset, ut Augustus potius vocaretur.

answer_en: On the motion of Munatius Plancus.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Bella civilia quinque gessit: Mutinense, Philippense, Perusinum, Siculum, Actiacum.

derivation: Source enumerates five named civil wars. Indirect statement (gessisse) under scribit; single number answer, entity-anchored.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Atque ab eo tempore exercitibus comparatis primum cum M. Antonio M. que Lepido deinde tantum cum Antonio per duodecim fere annos, novissime per quattuor et quadraginta solus rem publicam tenuit.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

derivation: Supported by 'Liviam Drusillam matrimonio Tiberi Neronis ... abduxit.' Entity-anchored (Augustus, Livia, her first husband), single answer.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius
source_text: Habuit in matrimonio Agrippinam, M. Agrippae et Iuliae filiam, et ex ea nouem liberos tulit.

derivation: Subject is Germanicus (from the preceding chapters). His wife and Caligula's mother is Agrippina the Elder, daughter of M. Agrippa and Iulia (Augustus's daughter). Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Germanicus/Caligula; single named answer with parentage; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Habuit in matrimonio Agrippinam, M. Agrippae et Iuliae filiam, et ex ea nouem liberos tulit.

derivation: Number fact, supported verbatim by 'ex ea nouem liberos tulit.' Entity-anchored to Germanicus and Agrippina; single-number answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Caligulae cognomen castrensi ioco traxit, quia manipulario habitu inter milites educabatur.

answer: Quia manipulario habitu inter milites educabatur.
question_en: Why did Gaius Caesar receive the nickname 'Caligula,' according to Suetonius?
answer_en: Because he was brought up among the soldiers dressed as a common soldier.
derivation: Origin of the famous nickname: a camp joke, because as a boy he was reared among the troops in a private soldier's outfit (the caligae, soldier's boots, give the name 'Caligula', little boot). Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula; closed-book (the etymology is the best-known fact about him); brief causal answer matching the source.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ego in actis Anti editum inuenio.

derivation: Suetonius, weighing conflicting traditions about Caligula's birthplace, settles on Antium on the authority of the public records (acta). Indirect statement (natum esse Gaium) under tradit; the attribution frame fits a claim Suetonius argues for. Place answer in the locative (Antii); entity-anchored, single answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: At in memoriam patris Septembrem mensem Germanicum appellauit.

derivation: He renamed September 'Germanicus' after his father. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula and Germanicus; single-month answer; closed-book, parallel to Augustus renaming Sextilis.

author: Suetonius
source_text: patruum Claudium, equitem R. ad id tempus, collegam sibi in consulatu assumpsit.

author: Suetonius

derivation: Number fact, supported verbatim by 'Consulatus quattuor gessit.' Entity-anchored to Caligula; single-number answer; closed-book.

derivation: Place fact: he entered his third consulship alone at Lugdunum. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula and the third consulship; single place answer in the locative (Luguduni).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Nam Baiarum medium interuallum ad Puteolanas moles, trium milium et sescentorum fere passuum spatium, ponte coniunxit contractis undique onerariis nauibus et ordine duplici ad anchoras conlocatis superiectoque terreno ac derecto in Appiae uiae formam.

answer_en: Between Baiae and the moles of Puteoli.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Incitato equo, cuius causa pridie circenses, ne inquietaretur, uiciniae silentium per milites indicere solebat, praeter equile marmoreum et praesaepe eburneum praeterque purpurea tegumenta ac monilia e gemmis domum etiam et familiam et supellectilem dedit, quo lautius nomine eius inuitati acciperentur; consulatum quoque traditur destinasse.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of February (24 January).
derivation: Date of the assassination: a.d. IX Kal. Feb. (= 24 January). Supported verbatim ('VIIII. Kal. Febr.'), the day on which, leaving for lunch, he was cut down. Entity-anchored to Caligula; single date answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius

derivation: Age-at-death fact, supported verbatim by 'Vixit annis uiginti nouem.' Entity-anchored to Caligula; single-number answer; closed-book.

answer_en: Three years, ten months, and eight days.
derivation: Reign-length fact, supported verbatim by 'imperauit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.' Answer kept in the ablative of duration as in the source. Entity-anchored to Caligula; precise span; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ex Antonia minore complures quidem liberos tulit, verum tres omnino reliquit: Germanicum, Livillam, Claudium.
question: Quis fuit frater maior Claudii imperatoris?
question_en: Who was the elder brother of the emperor Claudius?
derivation: Of Drusus and Antonia's three surviving children (Germanicus, Livilla, Claudius), Germanicus was the eldest; ch. 2 confirms 'fratre maiore.' Anchored to Claudius, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Claudius natus est Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss. Kal. Aug. Luguduni eo ipso die quo primum ara ibi Augusto dedicata est, appellatusque Tiberius Claudius Drusus.
question: In quo oppido natus est Claudius?
question_en: In what town was Claudius born?
derivation: Birthplace fact, supported by 'natus est ... Luguduni.' Single place-name answer, entity-anchored to Claudius; closed-book (he was the only emperor born in Gaul).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Claudius natus est Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss. Kal. Aug. Luguduni eo ipso die quo primum ara ibi Augusto dedicata est, appellatusque Tiberius Claudius Drusus.
question: Quibus consulibus natum esse Claudium Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In whose consulship does Suetonius say Claudius was born?
answer_en: When Iullus Antonius and Fabius Africanus were consuls.
derivation: Birth-year fact (10 BC). Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit; answer in the ablative matching 'Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss.' Entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Aviae Liviae diuinos honores et circensi pompa currum elephantorum Augustino similem decernenda curavit.
question: Cui aviae suae Claudius divinos honores decernendos curavit?
question_en: For which grandmother of his did Claudius see to it that divine honors were decreed?
derivation: Claudius consecrated his grandmother Livia (Augustus's wife), supported by 'Aviae Liviae diuinos honores ... decernenda curavit.' Names the grandmother plus a checkable act; entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Per haec ac talia maxima aetatis parte transacta quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit quantumuis mirabili casu.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Claudius imperium cepit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Claudius take power, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-accession fact, supported by 'quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored to Claudius, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum postero die et senatu segniore in exeqvendis conatibus per taedium ac dissensionem diversa censentium et multitudine, quae circumstabat, unum rectorem iam et nominatim exposcente, armatos pro contione iurare in nomen suum passus est promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.
question: Quantum praemium Claudius singulis militibus promisit, primus Caesarum fidem militis praemio pigneratus?
question_en: What bounty did Claudius promise to each soldier, being the first of the Caesars to secure the soldiers' loyalty even with a reward?
derivation: The accession donative to the praetorians who made him emperor; supported by 'promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to Claudius; closed-book (the famous first imperial accession donative).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cum decretis sibi a senatu ornamentis triumphalibus leviorem maiestati principali titulum arbitraretur velletque iusti triumphi decus, unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium et tunc tumultuantem ob non redditos transfugas.
question: Quam insulam Claudius, post Diuum Iulium a nullo temptatam, expeditione sua in deditionem recepit?
question_en: Which island, untried by anyone since the deified Julius, did Claudius receive in surrender by his expedition?
derivation: Claudius's annexation of Britain, his sole military expedition, supported by 'unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium.' Place answer, anchored to Claudius and Julius Caesar; iconic closed-book fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Fucinum adgressus est non minus conpendii spe quam gloriae, cum quidam privato sumptu emissuros se repromitterent, si sibi siccati agri concederentur. Per tria autem passuum milia partim effosso monte partim exciso canalem absoluit aegre et post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus sine intermissione operantibus.
question: Quot hominum milia Claudius in emissario Fucini lacus per undecim annos perficiendo adhibuit?
question_en: How many thousands of men did Claudius employ over eleven years to complete the outlet of the Fucine Lake?
derivation: The draining of Lake Fucinus, supported by 'post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus ... operantibus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to the Fucine project; closed-book engineering work.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
question: Quam gentem Claudius, impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantem, Roma expulit?
question_en: Which people, continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, did Claudius expel from Rome?
derivation: The expulsion of the Jews from Rome (cf. Acts 18:2), supported verbatim. Entity-anchored (Claudius + 'impulsore Chresto'), single-noun answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum inlecebris Agrippinae, Germanici fratris sui filiae, per ius osculi et blanditiarum occasiones pellectus in amorem, subornavit proximo senatu qui censerent, cogendum se ad ducendum eam uxorem, quasi rei p. maxime interesset, dandamque ceteris veniam talium coniugiorum, quae ad id tempus incesta habebantur.
question: Quam feminam, Germanici fratris sui filiam, Claudius novissimam uxorem duxit?
question_en: Which woman, the daughter of his brother Germanicus, did Claudius take as his last wife?
derivation: Claudius married his niece Agrippina the Younger (daughter of his brother Germanicus, and Nero's mother), supported by 'inlecebris Agrippinae, Germanici fratris sui filiae ... cogendum se ad ducendum eam uxorem.' Entity-anchored, surfaces the brother-relation, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Liberos ex tribus uxoribus tulit: ex Vrgulanilla Drusum et Claudiam, ex Paetina Antoniam, ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.
question: Quos liberos Claudius ex uxore Messalina suscepit?
question_en: Which children did Claudius have by his wife Messalina?
derivation: Supported by 'ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.' Names both children; entity-anchored to Claudius and Messalina; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Antoniam Cn. Pompeio Magno, deinde Fausto Sullae, nobilissimis iuvenibus, Octaviam Neroni priuigno suo collocavit, Silano ante desponsam.
question: Cui Claudius filiam Octaviam in matrimonium collocavit?
question_en: To whom did Claudius give his daughter Octavia in marriage?
derivation: Supported by 'Octaviam Neroni priuigno suo collocavit.' Nero was his stepson, adopted son, and successor. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: novas etiam commentus est litteras tres ac numero veterum quasi maxime necessarias addidit; de quarum ratione cum privatus adhuc volumen edidisset, mox princeps non difficulter optinuit ut in usu quoque promiscuo essent.
question: Quot novas litteras Claudius excogitavit et veterum numero addidit?
question_en: How many new letters did Claudius devise and add to the existing alphabet?
derivation: Claudius's three new letters added to the Latin alphabet, supported by 'novas etiam commentus est litteras tres ... addidit.' Number fact, entity-anchored, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Historiam in adulescentia hortante T. Livio, Sulpicio vero Flauo etiam adiuuante, scribere adgressus est.
question: Quo auctore hortante Claudius adulescens historiam scribere adgressus est?
question_en: At whose urging did the young Claudius undertake to write history?
derivation: Supported by 'Historiam in adulescentia hortante T. Livio ... scribere adgressus est.' Entity-anchored to Claudius and Livy, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Et veneno quidem occisum convenit; ubi autem et per quem dato, discrepat. Quidam tradunt epulanti in arce cum sacerdotibus per Halotum spadonem praegustatorem; alii domestico convivio per ipsam Agrippinam, quae boletum medicatum auidissimo ciborum talium optulerat.
question: Quo cibo medicato Claudius, ut plerique tradunt, veneno necatus est?
question_en: By which poisoned food, as most report, was Claudius killed?
derivation: The canonical account of Claudius's death by a poisoned mushroom offered by Agrippina, supported by 'veneno quidem occisum convenit ... per ipsam Agrippinam, quae boletum medicatum ... optulerat.' Entity-anchored, short answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Claudius decessit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Claudius die, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-death fact, supported by 'sexagesimo quarto aetatis.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Quoto imperii anno Claudius decessit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his reign did Claudius die, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Reign-length fact (AD 41-54), supported by 'imperii quarto decimo anno.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Per quem principem Claudius honorem divinum a Nerone abolitum recepit?
question_en: Through which emperor did Claudius regain the divine honor that Nero had abolished?
derivation: Claudius was deified at death; Nero let the honor lapse and Vespasian restored it, supported by 'in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.' Entity-anchored (Claudius, Nero, Vespasian), single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Domitianus natus est VIIII. Kal. Novemb. patre consule designato inituroque mense insequenti honorem, regione urbis sexta ad Malum Punicum, domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.
question: Quo die natum esse Domitianum Suetonius tradit?
answer: Ante diem nonum Kalendas Novembres (VIIII Kal. Novemb.).
question_en: On what day does Suetonius say Domitian was born?
answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of November (24 October).
derivation: Birth-date fact, anchored to Domitian. Supported verbatim by 'Domitianus natus est VIIII. Kal. Novemb.' Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit. Closed-book: the birth-date (24 October AD 51) of a major emperor; short calendrical answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: regione urbis sexta ad Malum Punicum, domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.
question: In quod templum Domitianus domum, in qua natus erat, postea convertit?
question_en: Into what temple did Domitian later convert the house in which he had been born?
answer_en: Into the temple of the Flavian gens.
derivation: Building/family fact: Domitian's birth-house (in Rome's sixth region) was later turned into the Templum Gentis Flaviae, the dynastic shrine of the Flavians. Supported verbatim by 'domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; single named-monument answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: contrectatis multorum uxoribus, Domitiam Longinam Aelio Lamiae nuptam etiam in matrimonium abduxit, atque uno die super XX. officia urbana aut peregrina distribuit.
question: Quam feminam, Aelio Lamiae nuptam, Domitianus in matrimonium abduxit?
question_en: Which woman, married to Aelius Lamia, did Domitian carry off into marriage?
derivation: Family fact: Domitian's wife was Domitia Longina, whom he took from her husband Aelius Lamia. Supported verbatim by 'Domitiam Longinam Aelio Lamiae nuptam etiam in matrimonium abduxit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Aelius Lamia; single-name answer; closed-book (Domitia Longina, daughter of Corbulo, is the well-known empress).

author: Suetonius
source_text: habitabat cum patre una, sellamque eius ac fratris, quotiens prodirent, lectica sequebatur ac triumphum utriusque Iudaicum equo albo comitatus est.
question: Quo equo Domitianus triumphum Iudaicum patris fratrisque comitatus est?
question_en: On what horse did Domitian accompany the Jewish triumph of his father and brother?
derivation: Career detail: Domitian rode a white horse in the Jewish triumph of his father Vespasian and brother Titus (AD 71). Supported verbatim by 'triumphum utriusque Iudaicum equo albo comitatus est.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + the Jewish triumph; short, concrete answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: nec quicquam amplius quam muscas captare ac stilo praeacuto configere; ut cuidam interroganti, essetne quis intus cum Caesare, non absurde responsum sit a Vibio Crispo, ne muscam quidem.
question: Quid Vibius Crispus respondit interroganti num quis intus cum Domitiano esset?
question_en: What did Vibius Crispus reply to the man who asked whether anyone was inside with Domitian?
derivation: Famous joke: Domitian spent his hours stabbing flies, so when asked if anyone was with Caesar, Vibius Crispus quipped 'not even a fly.' Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Vibius Crispus + Domitian; the witticism survives translation; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Instituit et quinquennale certamen Capitolino Iovi triplex, musicum, equestre, gymnicum, et aliquanto plurium quam nunc est coronatorum.
question: In cuius dei honorem Domitianus quinquennale certamen triplex instituit?
question_en: In whose honor did Domitian establish a triple quinquennial contest?
derivation: Institutional fact: Domitian founded the quinquennial Capitoline Games (musical, equestrian, gymnastic) in honor of Capitoline Jupiter. Supported verbatim by 'quinquennale certamen Capitolino Iovi triplex.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Capitoline Jupiter; single-name answer; the Agon Capitolinus is a recognized institution.

author: Suetonius
source_text: De Chattis Dacisque post varia proelia duplicem triumphum egit.
question: De quibus gentibus Domitianus duplicem triumphum egit?
question_en: Over which peoples did Domitian celebrate a double triumph?
answer_en: Over the Chatti and the Dacians.
derivation: Military fact: a double triumph over the Chatti and the Dacians. Supported verbatim by 'De Chattis Dacisque ... duplicem triumphum egit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + named peoples; short list answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Bellum civile motum a L. Antonio, superioris Germaniae praeside, confecit absens felicitate mira.
question: Quis, superioris Germaniae praeses, bellum civile adversus Domitianum movit?
question_en: Who, as governor of Upper Germany, stirred up civil war against Domitian?
derivation: Historical fact: the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus, governor of Upper Germany (AD 89), put down in Domitian's absence. Supported verbatim by 'Bellum civile motum a L. Antonio, superioris Germaniae praeside.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + the office; single-name answer (cognomen Saturninus supplied only in the gloss, not the text).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Iunium Rusticum, quod Paeti Thraseae et Helvidii Prisci laudes edidisset appellassetque eos sanctissimos viros; cuius criminis occasione philosophos omnis urbe Italiaque summovit.
question: Quos Domitianus, occasione damnati Iunii Rustici, urbe Italiaque summovit?
question_en: Whom did Domitian expel from Rome and Italy, on the occasion of the condemnation of Junius Rusticus?
derivation: Historical fact: Domitian's expulsion of philosophers from Rome and Italy, occasioned by the condemnation of Junius Rusticus (who had praised Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus). Supported verbatim by 'philosophos omnis urbe Italiaque summovit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Junius Rusticus; short answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Pari arrogantia, cum procuratorum suorum nomine formalem dictaret epistulam, sic coepit: "Dominus et deus noster hoc fieri iubet." Vnde institutum posthac, ut ne scripto quidem ac sermone cuiusquam appellaretur aliter.
question: Quibus verbis se appellari Domitianus voluit, cum epistulam procuratorum suorum nomine dictaret?
question_en: By what words did Domitian want himself to be addressed, when he dictated a letter in the name of his procurators?
derivation: Iconic fact: Domitian had himself styled 'dominus et deus,' beginning an official letter 'Our lord and god orders this,' and thereafter was addressed no otherwise. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Domitian; the title survives translation; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Consulatus septemdecim cepit, quot ante eum nemo; ex quibus septem medios continuavit, omnes autem paene titulo tenus gessit.
question: Quot consulatus Domitianus cepit, quot ante eum nemo gesserat?
question_en: How many consulships did Domitian hold, more than anyone before him?
derivation: Number fact: Domitian held seventeen consulships, more than any predecessor. Supported verbatim by 'Consulatus septemdecim cepit, quot ante eum nemo.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; single-number answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Post autem duos triumphos Germanici cognomine assumpto Septembrem mensem et Octobrem ex appellationibus suis Germanico Domitianumque transnominavit, quod altero suscepisset imperium, altero natus esset.
question: In quae nomina Domitianus menses Septembrem et Octobrem transnominavit?
answer: Septembrem in Germanicum, Octobrem in Domitianum.
question_en: Into what names did Domitian rename the months of September and October?
derivation: Naming fact: Domitian renamed September 'Germanicus' (the month he had taken up the empire) and October 'Domitianus' (the month he was born). Supported verbatim by 'Septembrem mensem et Octobrem ... Germanico Domitianumque transnominavit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; short paired answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Per haec terribilis cunctis et invisus, tandem oppressus est amicorum libertorumque intimorum conspiratione, simul et uxoris.
question: Qua coniuratione Domitianus tandem oppressus est?
answer: Amicorum libertorumque intimorum, simul et uxoris.
question_en: By what conspiracy was Domitian at last overthrown?
answer_en: By a conspiracy of his intimate friends and freedmen, together with his wife.
derivation: Death fact: Domitian was killed by a palace conspiracy of his closest friends and freedmen, joined by his wife. Supported verbatim by 'oppressus est amicorum libertorumque intimorum conspiratione, simul et uxoris.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; short phrase answer; closed-book (the assassination of AD 96).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Stephanus, Domitillae procurator, et tunc interceptarum pecuniarum reus, consilium operamque optulit. Ac sinisteriore brachio, velut aegro, lanis fasciisque per aliquot dies ad avertendam suspicionem obvoluto, ad ipsam horam dolorem interiecit; professusque conspirationis indicium et ob hos admissus, legenti traditum a se libellum et attonito suffodit inguina.
question: Quis Domitiano, legenti libellum, primum vulnus intulit, inguina suffodiens?
question_en: Who struck the first blow at Domitian, stabbing him in the groin while he read a document?
derivation: Assassination fact: the steward Stephanus struck the first blow, stabbing Domitian in the groin as he read a handed-over document. Supported verbatim by 'Stephanus, Domitillae procurator ... legenti traditum a se libellum et attonito suffodit inguina.' Entity-anchored; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Occisus est XIIII. Kal. Octob. anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto, imperii quinto decimo.
question: Quotum aetatis annum agens Domitianus occisus est?
question_en: In which year of his age was Domitian killed?
derivation: Age-at-death fact. Supported verbatim by 'anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Domitian; closed-book (killed AD 96, aged 44/45). Source retains the Latin Library spelling 'quadragensimo' for 'quadragesimo.'

author: Suetonius
source_text: Occisus est XIIII. Kal. Octob. anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto, imperii quinto decimo.
question: Quoto imperii anno Domitianus occisus est?
question_en: In which year of his reign was Domitian killed?
derivation: Reign-length fact: Domitian was killed in the fifteenth year of his reign (AD 81-96). Supported verbatim by 'imperii quinto decimo.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Domitian; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Contra senatus adeo laetatus est, ut repleta certatim curia non temperaret, quin mortuum contumeliosissimo atque acerbissimo adclamationum genere laceraret, scalas etiam inferri clipeosque et imagines eius coram detrahi et ibidem solo affligi iuberet, novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.
question: Quid senatus de Domitiano occiso decrevit, titulos eius ubique eradi iubens?
question_en: What did the senate decree about the slain Domitian, ordering his inscriptions to be erased everywhere?
answer_en: That all memory of him be abolished (the damnatio memoriae).
derivation: Historical fact: the senate rejoiced at Domitian's death and decreed his inscriptions erased and all memory of him abolished (damnatio memoriae). Supported verbatim by 'novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.' Entity-anchored to the senate + Domitian; short noun-phrase answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
